name: Genesis
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: In the beginning,{a} God{b} made heaven and earth.
The earth was a shapeless, empty place. Black darkness lay on the deep waters, and God’s Spirit{c} swept back and forth above them.
God spoke: “Light, shine out!” And light shone.
The light was good, God saw. He set the light apart from the dark.
The light he called Day, and the dark he called Night. Dusk fell, and then dawn came. That was day one.{d}
God said, “Let a wide space{e} open up inside the waters, so that some waters are held apart from others.”
God made that space. The waters under it were now apart from the waters above it. It was so.
God called the space Sky. Dusk fell, and then dawn came. That was the second day of creation.
Then God spoke: “Waters under the sky, gather in a single place! Let dry ground come into view.” So it was.
The dry ground became “Land” and the gathered waters became “Seas,” as God named them. He looked, and he was pleased.
God ordered, “Let the land sprout green things: grasses and plants that carry seeds, and trees that bear fruit with seeds inside. Each one will grow from its own kind of seed.” So it was.
The land sprouted grasses and plants with seeds, and trees that bore fruit with seeds inside, each after its own kind. God looked, and he was pleased.
Dusk fell, and then dawn came. That was the third day.
God declared, “Let lights shine in the sky’s wide space, to cut the day off from the night. They will mark the seasons,{f} and they will count off the days and years.
They will hang in the sky and light up the earth.” So it was.
God made two bright lamps. The brighter one would govern the day, and the dimmer one would govern the night.{g} The stars were his work too.
He hung them high in the sky so they would shine down on the world.
These lamps would rule over each day and each night, and they would keep light and dark apart. God looked, and he was pleased.
Dusk fell, and then dawn came. That was the fourth day.
God commanded, “Let the waters teem with living creatures, and let birds soar across the open sky above the earth.”
God made the giant animals of the sea,{h} and every kind of living thing that glides or swarms through the water. Every kind of winged bird was his work too. God looked, and he was pleased.
God blessed them. He said, “Bear young and grow in number. Fill the seas! Let the birds fill the land with their young.”
Dusk fell, and then dawn came. That was the fifth day.
God said, “Now let animals of many kinds come out of the ground: cattle, creatures that creep, and wild beasts.” So it was.
God made wild beasts, cattle, and all the creatures that creep, each in its own kind. God looked, and he was pleased.

God now said, “Let us make human beings,{i} who will be like us and look like us. Let them be the rulers over the fish of the water and the birds of the air, over the farm animals and wild beasts, and over every small creature that creeps along the ground.”
So God made human beings to be like himself. He made them to carry the likeness of God. He made a man and a woman.{j}

God blessed them. “Have children,” he said, “and grow in number until the earth is full. Look after it and bring it under your care. You are the rulers of the fish in the water, of the birds in the air, and of every creature that lives and moves on the land.”
God also said, “Here is your food: every plant that makes seed, all over the earth, and every tree whose fruit has seed in it.
For the wild beasts, for the birds, and for everything that creeps on the ground, for every living thing that breathes, I give the green plants as food.” So it was.
God looked over his whole creation, and it was very good indeed. Dusk fell, and then dawn came. That was the sixth day.

notes.text: Hebrew bereshit. Some read it as the start of a longer sentence: “When God began to make the sky and the earth…”
Hebrew Elohim. It is a title, “God,” not a personal name. It looks plural in Hebrew, but it takes a singular verb here, so it means the one God.
Hebrew ruach means “spirit,” “wind,” or “breath.” Some Bibles read “a mighty wind.”
Literally “day one.” The Hebrew uses the number one, not “first.”
Hebrew raqia. It comes from a word for beating metal flat, so it means something stretched out. Old Bibles say “firmament.”
Hebrew moadim, “appointed times.” The same word is later used for Israel’s holy festivals.
The sun and moon are not named here. Neighbors of Israel worshiped them as gods, but here they are only lights God made.
Hebrew tanninim, a word used for sea monsters elsewhere. Even these are just creatures God made.
Hebrew adam, the word for the human race. It later becomes the name Adam.
The Hebrew moves from “him” to “them.” One human race, made male and female.

verses.text: In this way the sky and the earth were finished, together with all that fills them.
When the seventh day came, God’s work was done, and on that day he stopped and rested.{a}
God gave the seventh day his blessing and made it holy. It was the day he took a break from all the making he had done.
Here is the account of how heaven and earth came to be. Yahweh{b} God had just made them.
Not one wild bush had come up yet, and no field crops were growing. Yahweh God had not yet sent rain, and no one was there to work the soil.
But a stream of water{c} would come up out of the earth and soak the ground everywhere.
Then Yahweh God scooped up dust from the soil and shaped{d} a man. This man was Adam.{e} God blew the breath of life into Adam’s nose, and the man came alive.
Yahweh God also planted a garden. It was in Eden,{f} far to the east. That is where he placed the man he had shaped.

All kinds of trees sprouted there at Yahweh God’s word. Each one was a pleasure to see, and its fruit was good for eating. In the very center grew two special trees: the tree of life, and the tree of knowing good and evil.{g}
A river started in Eden and ran through the garden. Past the garden, it split into four branches.
The first stream is named Pishon. It circles the whole country of Havilah, a land that has gold.
The gold from that country is excellent. Fragrant gum and onyx stone{h} come from there as well.
The second stream is named Gihon. It circles the entire country of Cush.{i}
The third stream is named Tigris, and it passes east of Assyria. The fourth stream is the Euphrates.
Yahweh God took Adam and put him in Eden’s garden, to till the soil and guard it.{j}
Yahweh God gave Adam an order. “Eat as much as you like from any of the garden’s trees.{k}
But there is one tree you must leave alone: the tree of knowing good and evil. Eat its fruit, and on that very day you will die.”{l}
Then Yahweh God said, “Adam should not be alone. That is not good. I will make him a partner who suits him, someone to stand beside him.”{m}
Yahweh God had formed each wild animal and each bird out of the ground. Now he led them to Adam, to watch what names Adam would choose. Whatever Adam called a creature became its name.
So Adam gave a name to each of the cattle, each bird in the sky, and each beast of the wild. Yet for Adam{n} none of them was the partner he needed.
Next, Yahweh God made Adam sleep deeply. While Adam slept, God took one rib{o} from Adam and sealed the gap with flesh.
From that rib, Yahweh God built a woman and presented her to Adam.
Adam cried out, “This is the one! Her bones are my bones, her flesh is my flesh. Woman is her name, because out of Man she was taken.”{p}
That is the reason a man leaves behind his father and mother, and holds tightly to his wife. The two become a single body.{q}
Adam and his wife were bare, and yet neither one was ashamed.

notes.text: Hebrew shavat means “stopped.” It is the root of the word “Sabbath.” The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Syriac say “on the sixth day” in 2:2.
Yahweh is God’s personal name, written YHWH in Hebrew. This is the first time it appears. See Exodus 3:14–15.
Hebrew ed is a rare word. It may mean a spring or a stream under the ground.
Hebrew yatsar is the word for a potter shaping clay. This is the picture of the “clay jar.”
Adam sounds like Hebrew adamah, “ground.” The name means “human” or “man from the ground.”
Eden probably means “delight” or “plenty.”
This may mean knowing everything, or deciding for yourself what is right and wrong.
Hebrew bdellium (a sweet-smelling resin) and shoham. The stone is uncertain; it may be onyx or carnelian.
Cush is usually the land south of Egypt. Here it may be a different place.
Hebrew avad and shamar, “serve” and “guard.” Priests later use the same pair of words for their work at the sanctuary.
Literally “eating you may eat,” a strong way of saying “freely.”
Literally “dying you will die.” The serpent repeats and denies these words in 3:4.
Hebrew ezer kenegdo. The word ezer, “helper,” is often used for God helping his people. It does not mean a lesser person.
Here the Hebrew may use “Adam” as a personal name, not just “the man.”
Hebrew tsela usually means “side.” It is the same word used for the side of the tent of meeting.
In Hebrew the words sound alike: ishshah, “woman,” and ish, “man.”
Some old copies, such as the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint, add “the two” before “become one.” Matthew 19:5 quotes it that way.

verses.text: Yahweh God had made many wild creatures, and the snake was the craftiest{a} of them all. It said to the woman, “Did God truly tell you, ‘You may not eat from any tree in the garden’?”
The woman told it, “Oh no, the fruit from the garden’s trees is ours to eat.
God only spoke against the tree in the middle. He said, ‘Do not eat from it, or even touch it, or death will come to you.’”
“Die? Never!” said the snake.
“God knows better. When you eat from that tree, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God,{b} able to tell good from evil.”

The woman looked at the tree. Its fruit seemed good to eat, it was a joy to see, and it promised to make her wise. So she picked some and ate it. Then she handed some to her husband, who stood beside her, and he ate too.
At once their eyes were opened, and they realized they had no clothes on. They stitched fig leaves together and wrapped them around themselves.
In the cool of the afternoon, the man and his wife heard Yahweh God strolling through the garden.{c} They slipped in among the trees to hide from him.
Yahweh God called out to the man, “Where are you?”
Adam replied, “Your voice reached me in the garden, and fear came over me, because I had nothing on. So I hid.”
God said, “Who told you that you were bare? Have you eaten fruit from the one tree I ordered you to avoid?”
Adam said, “The woman you placed next to me is to blame. She gave me fruit from that tree, and I ate it.”
Yahweh God turned to the woman. “What is it you did?” She replied, “The snake cheated me,{d} and I ate.”
Then Yahweh God spoke to the snake: “You did this, and so you are cursed above every farm animal and every wild creature. Your belly will drag the ground, and dust will be your meal all your days.
I will turn you and the woman into enemies, and your children and hers into enemies too.{e} He will strike at your head, and you will strike at his heel.”
To the woman he said, “Your pain in pregnancy{f} will be very great, and you will bear children in agony. Yet you will crave your husband,{g} and he will rule over you.”

To Adam he said, “You obeyed your wife’s voice and ate from the tree I had forbidden. For that reason the soil is cursed. Hard labor and sweat{h} will be the price of every meal you take from it, for the rest of your life.
Thorn bushes and thistles will sprout in it, and your food will be the crops of the field.
Sweat will drip from your face as you eat. That will go on until you go back to the earth, since the earth is where you came from. You are made of dust, and dust is where you will end up.”
The man called his wife Eve,{i} since she was going to be the mother of every living person.
Yahweh God made coats of animal skin for Adam and his wife, and he helped them put them on.
Yahweh God said, “Now the man is like one of us, knowing good and evil. I cannot let him reach for the tree of life, eat from it, and live without end.”{j}
So Yahweh God drove him out of Eden’s garden, to farm the same ground he was taken from.

After he drove Adam out, God stationed winged guardians,{k} the cherubim, east of the garden. A flaming sword also flashed there, whirling in every direction,{l} so no one could reach the tree of life.

notes.text: Hebrew arum, “clever” or “sly.” It sounds like arummim, “naked,” in 2:25.
Hebrew elohim can mean “God,” “gods,” or “heavenly beings.” The Septuagint says “like gods.”
Or “voice.” The same Hebrew word is used again in 3:10.
The Hebrew word means “led me wrong” or “fooled me.” Paul refers to this in 2 Corinthians 11:3.
Literally “seed.” The word can mean one child or many. The Septuagint and Hebrew both say “he.”
Literally “your pain and your pregnancy.”
The Septuagint says “you will turn to your husband.” The Hebrew word is also used in 4:7.
Hebrew itstsavon, “hard work” or “pain.” It is the same word used for the woman’s pain in 3:16.
Hebrew Chavvah, which sounds like the word for “life.”
The sentence is not finished in Hebrew. Verse 23 shows what God did.
Cherubim is the Hebrew plural of cherub. They are winged beings who guard holy places.
Literally “the blade of the flame, turning itself about.”

verses.text: Adam was united with his wife Eve,{a} and she conceived. She gave birth to a son, Cain,{b} and declared, “With Yahweh’s help, I have brought forth a man!”
Next she bore his brother Abel.{c} Abel tended the sheep, and Cain worked the soil.
Some time later, Cain presented part of his harvest to Yahweh as a gift.
Abel, too, offered a gift: the best of his firstborn lambs, with their fat. Yahweh was delighted with Abel and his gift,
but he turned away from Cain and his gift. Cain burned with anger, and he scowled.
Yahweh asked Cain, “Why this rage? Why the scowl on your face?
If you do right, you can look up again.{d} If not, sin is crouching at your door, like a beast ready to pounce. It longs to master you, yet you can master it.”
One day Cain said to his brother Abel, “Come, let us walk out into the countryside.”{e} Out there, Cain turned on Abel and murdered him.
Yahweh then asked, “Where is Abel, your brother?” “How should I know?” Cain answered. “Am I my brother’s guard?”{f}
Yahweh said, “What have you done? Hark! From the ground, your brother’s blood is shouting to me!
Now a curse is on you. The ground opened wide to receive your brother’s blood, which your hand spilled, and now it is closed to you.
When you farm it from now on, it will refuse to give you a harvest. You will drift from place to place, never at rest.”{g}
Cain said to Yahweh, “I cannot bear a punishment this heavy.{h}
Look, you are throwing me off this land today, and I must hide away from you. I will roam the earth with no home, and whoever finds me will kill me.”
Yahweh said, “No. If anyone kills Cain, he will be repaid seven times over.” And Yahweh marked{i} Cain, to protect him from anyone who might meet him.
So Cain walked away from Yahweh and settled in the land of Nod,{j} which lies east of Eden.
Cain’s wife conceived, and Enoch{k} was her son. Cain was constructing a city at the time, and he named it for his son Enoch.
Enoch’s son was Irad. Irad’s son was Mehujael, and Mehujael’s son was Methushael. Methushael’s son was Lamech.
Two women became Lamech’s wives: Adah and Zillah.
Adah’s son Jabal became the father of tent dwellers and cattle keepers.
His brother Jubal was the ancestor of every lyre player and pipe player.{l}
Zillah’s son was Tubal-cain, who made every kind of tool from bronze and iron. Naamah was Tubal-cain’s sister.
Lamech said to his wives, “Adah and Zillah, hear me! Wives of Lamech, take in my words! I have slain a man who wounded me, a youth who struck me.
If Cain gets seven times payback, then Lamech gets seventy-seven times!”{m}
Adam was united with his wife again, and she bore him a son. She named him Seth.{n} “Abel is gone, killed by Cain,” she said, “but God has given me another child to take his place.”
A son was also born to Seth, and he called the boy Enosh.{o} At that time people started to call on Yahweh by name.{p}

notes.text: Literally “Adam knew Eve.” “Know” is a common Hebrew word for married love.
Cain (Hebrew Qayin) sounds like “I have gained.” The name may also mean “metalworker.”
Abel (Hebrew Hevel) means “breath” or “puff of wind.” It hints at how short his life was.
Hebrew seet, “a lifting.” It can mean “accepted,” “forgiven,” or “face lifted up.” The meaning is hard to be sure of.
The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Syriac have Cain speaking to Abel here. Most Hebrew copies do not give his words.
The Hebrew word for “watch over” is the same word used for “take care of” in 2:15.
Hebrew na wanad, a pair of rhyming words meaning “wanderer.” It leads to the name of the land Nod.
Hebrew avon means both guilt and its punishment. It can also mean “My sin is too big to be forgiven.”
Hebrew ot, “sign.” It was a mark that protected him, not one of shame.
Nod means “wandering.”
Enoch (Hebrew Chanokh) may mean “dedicated.” This is Cain’s son, not the Enoch of chapter 5.
Hebrew kinnor, a stringed instrument, and ugav, probably a flute.
Hebrew “seventy-sevenfold.” Jesus said to forgive “seventy-seven times” in Matthew 18:22.
Seth (Hebrew Shet) sounds like “he has given.”
Enosh means “human” or “mortal.”
Literally “then it was begun to call on the name of Yahweh.” The Septuagint reads “he hoped to call on the name of the Lord God.”

verses.text: Here is the written record of Adam’s descendants.{a} In the day God shaped humanity, he patterned them after himself.
Male and female were his design. He gave them his blessing and named the pair “Adam,”{b} a word that means human.
Adam was 130 years old{c} when a son was born who looked just like him. Adam called the boy Seth.{d}
After that, Adam lived 800 more years, and sons and daughters were born to him.
Adam’s whole life added up to 930 years, and then death came.
Seth was 105 years old when Enosh became his son.
For 807 years afterward Seth kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Altogether, Seth lived 912 years, and then death came.
Enosh was 90 years old when Kenan{e} became his son.
For 815 years afterward Enosh kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Altogether, Enosh lived 905 years, and then death came.
Kenan was 70 years old when Mahalalel{f} became his son.
For 840 years afterward Kenan kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Altogether, Kenan lived 910 years, and then death came.
Mahalalel was 65 years old when Jared{g} became his son.
For 830 years afterward Mahalalel kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Altogether, Mahalalel lived 895 years, and then death came.
Jared was 162 years old when Enoch became his son.
For 800 years afterward Jared kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Altogether, Jared lived 962 years, and then death came.
Enoch was 65 years old when Methuselah{h} became his son.
For 300 years afterward Enoch walked close with God,{i} and he fathered sons and daughters.
Enoch’s life lasted 365 years in all.{j}
Enoch walked close with God, and then he could not be found, for God had taken him away.{k}
Methuselah was 187 years old when Lamech became his son.
For 782 years afterward Methuselah kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Altogether, Methuselah lived 969 years, and then death came.{l}
Lamech was 182 years old when a son was born to him.
He named the boy Noah.{m} “This child will give us relief,” Lamech said, “from the hard labor and sore hands we get from farming the ground that Yahweh cursed.”
For 595 years after Noah was born, Lamech kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Altogether, Lamech lived 777 years, and then death came.
Noah was 500 years old when he became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.{n}

notes.text: Hebrew sefer toledot, “the book of the family line.” Matthew 1:1 begins the New Testament in a similar way.
Hebrew adam. In verses 1–2 it means all people; from verse 3 it is the man’s name.

Hebrew writes numbers as words. This Bible uses figures to make them easy to read. The ages in this chapter differ in the Hebrew, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the Septuagint, and no Dead Sea Scroll has them.
Seth sounds like Hebrew “he has granted.”
Kenan (Hebrew Qenan) is close to the name Cain.
Mahalalel means “praise of God.”
Jared probably means “descent.”
Methuselah probably means “man of the spear” or “man of Shelah.”
Literally “walked about with God.” It pictures close, everyday friendship. The Septuagint says “pleased God.”
This is the number of days in a year.
Literally “he was not.” The same verb “took” is used for Elijah in 2 Kings 2. The Septuagint says “he was not found, because God moved him.”
By the Hebrew numbers, Methuselah died in the year of the flood. The Septuagint numbers would have him live 14 years past it.
Noah (Hebrew Noach) sounds like words for “rest” and “comfort.” The Septuagint says “will give us rest.”
Shem means “name.” Ham may mean “hot.” The sons may not be listed in order of age.

verses.text: People were spreading out over the earth, and daughters were being born to them.
The sons of God{a} looked at the human daughters and thought they were lovely, so they married whichever ones they liked.
Then Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not stay{b} with people forever, for they are only flesh.{c} Their lives will be limited to 120 years.”{d}
In those days, and later too, the Nephilim{e} lived on the earth. They were born when the sons of God slept with human women. These were the heroes{f} of long ago, the famous men.{g}
Yahweh saw that people on earth were very wicked. Every plan{h} their hearts made was bad, all the time.
Yahweh’s heart ached.{i} He regretted that he had ever made people on earth, and it hurt him deeply.{j}
He said, “I will sweep from the earth the people I made: people, animals, crawling things, and birds. I am sorry I made them.”
But Noah had won Yahweh’s kindness.{k}
Here is Noah’s story. He was a good man, and in his time he was the only one with a clean record.{l} Noah walked close with God.{m}
He was the father of three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
Meanwhile, the earth had become rotten{n} in God’s sight and was packed with violence.{o}
When God looked over the earth, he saw how spoiled it was. Everyone on it had ruined their way of life.
So God told Noah, “I have decided to end every living creature,{p} since violence fills the earth because of them. They and the earth will go down in ruin together.
Build yourself a boat, an ark,{q} from gopher wood.{r} Divide it into rooms, and seal it with tar{s} on the inside and the outside.
Here is the plan. Make the ark 450 feet in length, 75 feet in width, and 45 feet in height.{t}
Give it a roof,{u} leaving a gap of about eighteen inches below the top. Set a door in the side. Give it three floors: a bottom, a middle, and a top.
I am about to send a flood{v} of water over the earth. It will wipe out everything that breathes under the sky. All life on earth will end.
But with you I will make a promise.{w} You will enter the ark, along with your wife, your sons, and their wives.
Bring two of every living creature on board, a male and a female, to keep them alive with you.
A pair of every bird, of every farm animal, and of every crawling creature will come to you, so that they stay alive.
Also gather every kind of edible food and store it away, so there will be enough for you and for the animals.”
Noah carried out every detail, just as God had ordered.

notes.text: Hebrew bene ha-elohim. It may mean heavenly beings, as in Job 1:6. Others think it means rulers or the family line of Seth.
Hebrew yadon is a rare word and its meaning is uncertain. The Septuagint and Vulgate read “stay.”
Or “because they went astray.”
This may be the limit of a human life, or the time left before the flood.
Nephilim is left as it is. It may mean “fallen ones” or “those who attack.” The Septuagint says “giants.”
Hebrew gibborim, “warriors” or “heroes.”
Literally “men of the name.” Compare the builders in 11:4 who want to “make a name.”
Hebrew yetser, “what is formed,” from the same root as “shaped” in 2:7.
Hebrew nacham can mean “be sorry,” “change one’s mind,” or “be comforted.” It sounds like the name Noah.
From the same root as “pain” in 3:16–17 and 5:29.
Hebrew chen, “favor” or “kindness.” Its letters are Noah’s name written backward.
Hebrew tamim, “complete” or “sound.” It was used for animals without a flaw. It does not mean never sinning (see 9:21).
Noah’s “walk” is the same as Enoch’s in 5:22.
Hebrew shachat, “spoiled.” The same word is used for “destroy” in verses 13 and 17.
Hebrew chamas, harsh and cruel wrongdoing.
Literally “the end of all flesh has come before me.” The meaning is that God has decided to end all living things.
Hebrew tevah, a box. The only other time it is used is for the basket of baby Moses in Exodus 2:3–5.
The wood is not known. It may be cypress. The Septuagint says “squared timber.”
Hebrew kofer, from a word meaning “to cover.” It is a root later used for atonement.
Hebrew “300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high.” A cubit is about 18 inches, or 45 cm.
Hebrew tsohar, found only here. It may mean a roof or a window. Literally the gap is “a cubit,” about 18 inches.
Hebrew mabbul, a word used almost only for this flood.
Hebrew berit, usually “covenant.” This is the first use of the word in the Bible. It is carried out in 9:8–17.

verses.text: Yahweh said to Noah, “Enter the ark with all your family. I have seen that in this age you alone are good before me.
Take seven pairs{a} from each kind of clean animal, each a male with its mate. From each kind that is not clean, take one pair, a male with its mate.
Bring seven pairs of the sky’s birds as well, males and females,{b} to keep each kind alive over all the earth.
One week from now I will send rain on the earth for forty days and forty nights. I will erase from the ground every living thing{c} I have made.”
Noah did everything Yahweh ordered.
Noah had lived 600 years when the great flood came upon the earth.
Noah, his wife, his sons, and his sons’ wives boarded the ark to get away from the flood.
The clean animals and the unclean, the birds, and every creature that creeps along the ground
came to Noah in pairs, male and female, as God had commanded.
After the seven days, the floodwaters came.
In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, on the seventeenth day of the second month (in April–May),{d} the springs of the great deep burst wide and the sky’s floodgates{e} swung open.
The rain kept falling on the earth, forty days and nights without a break.
That very day, Noah entered the ark along with his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and his wife and his three daughters-in-law.
With them came every kind of wild animal, every kind of farm animal, every kind of crawling creature, and every kind of bird, every winged thing.{f}
Pair by pair they came to Noah and boarded the ark, every creature that breathed.
The animals that entered, a male and a female of each kind, went in as God had ordered. Then Yahweh closed the door behind Noah.{g}
For forty days{h} the flood kept coming. The water rose and lifted the ark high off the ground.
The water kept growing{i} and climbing, and the ark floated on top of it.
The water grew higher and higher until it covered all the tall mountains under the whole sky.
It rose about 22 feet over the mountaintops.{j}
Everything that moved on the earth died: birds, farm animals, wild animals, every small creature that swarms, and every human being.
Everything on dry land that breathed the breath of life through its nose died.{k}
Yahweh erased every living thing from the earth: people, animals, crawling things, and birds. All were gone. Only Noah was left, and those who shared the ark with him.
The water stayed high over the earth for 150 days.{l}

notes.text: Literally “seven seven.” It may mean seven pairs, or seven animals. The Septuagint says “seven seven” too.
The Septuagint adds “of the clean birds” and then lists pairs of the birds that are not clean.
Hebrew yequm, a rare word meaning “everything that stands” or “everything that exists.”
Hebrew “the second month.” This Bible counts months from the spring new year (Nisan, March–April). Some count from autumn, which would make this month October–November.
Hebrew arubbot, “windows” or “lattices,” a picture of the sky as a dome with openings.
Literally “every bird, every wing.”
The verse changes from “God” to “Yahweh.”
The Septuagint reads “forty days and forty nights.”
Hebrew gavar, “grew strong.” It is used four times in verses 18–24.
Hebrew “fifteen cubits upward,” about 22 feet (7 meters).
Literally “in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life.”
Five months of 30 days, from the seventeenth day of the second month (7:11) to the seventeenth day of the seventh month (8:4).

verses.text: But God had not forgotten{a} Noah, or the wild animals and farm animals that shared the ark with him. He sent a wind{b} across the earth, and the water began to sink.
The deep’s springs and the sky’s floodgates were closed, and the rain from the clouds stopped.
Little by little the water drained off the land.{c} After 150 days it had dropped low.
On the seventeenth day of the seventh month (in September–October),{d} the ark came to rest{e} among the mountains of Ararat.{f}
The water kept dropping until the tenth month (in December–January). On the first day of that month,{g} the mountain peaks came into view.
After forty days, Noah unlatched the window he had built into the ark.
He let a raven fly out. It flew back and forth{h} until the earth was dry.
Next Noah released a dove, to find out whether the ground was clear of water.
The dove found nowhere to land{i} because water still covered the whole earth, so it flew back to the ark. Noah reached out, caught it, and brought it inside.
Seven days passed, and again he sent the dove out.
At evening the dove flew back to him, and in its beak was a newly picked olive leaf. From this Noah understood that the water had left the earth.
He waited seven days more and sent the dove out a third time. It never came back to him.
In Noah’s six hundred and first year,{j} on the first day of the first month (in March–April),{k} the earth’s water was gone. Noah pulled back the ark’s cover and looked around. The ground was dry!
By the twenty-seventh day of the second month (in April–May), the land was fully dry.{l}
Then God said to Noah,
“Step out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives.
Lead out all the creatures that are with you: birds, farm animals, and everything that crawls. Let them swarm over the land, bearing young and multiplying.”
So Noah came out, accompanied by his wife, his sons, and their wives.
Every animal, every crawling thing, and every bird, all that move on the earth, left the ark, kind by kind.
Noah built an altar for Yahweh. He chose some of the clean animals and clean birds and burned them whole on the altar as an offering.

Yahweh enjoyed the pleasing smell.{m} Then he thought, “Never again will I put the ground under a curse for people’s sake, though their hearts lean toward evil from childhood.{n} Never again will I strike down all living things the way I have done.
While the earth endures,{o} seed and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will not come to an end.”

notes.text: Hebrew zakar. When God “remembers” in the Bible, he acts to help. It does not mean he had forgotten.
Hebrew ruach, “wind” or “spirit,” as in 1:2.
Literally “going and returning.”
Hebrew “the seventh month.” This Bible counts months from the spring new year (see the note on 7:11).
Hebrew wattanach, from nuach, “rest.” It sounds like the name Noah.
Ararat is a region in what is now eastern Turkey and Armenia. The text says “mountains,” not one peak.
Hebrew “the tenth month,” counted from spring.
Literally “going out and returning.” The Septuagint says the raven “did not return.”
Hebrew manoach, again from nuach, “rest.”
The Septuagint says “the six hundred and first year of Noah’s life.”
Hebrew “the first month,” counted from spring (see the note on 7:11). In the autumn calendar it would be September–October.
Hebrew “the second month,” counted from spring. This is a year and ten days after the flood began.
Hebrew reach ha-nichoach, “the restful smell,” another sound-play on Noah’s name.
Or “since the human heart is evil from youth.” It is the same sad fact as in 6:5, but now it leads to mercy.
Literally “all the days of the earth.” The verse is a short poem of pairs.

verses.text: God blessed Noah and his sons. He told them, “Have children, and fill the earth.
All the land animals, every bird of the sky, everything that crawls, and all the fish of the sea will tremble before you. They are in your hands now.
Everything that moves and lives may be food for you, as the green plants were. Now I give you all of it.
But never eat meat that still has its life in it, which is its blood.{a}
I will demand payment for your lifeblood, too.{b} I will demand it from any animal, and from any person who takes a human life.{c}
If someone sheds a person’s blood, a person will shed his.{d} For God made humans like himself.
As for you, bear many children and fill the earth with them.”{e}
God also spoke to Noah and his sons:
“Listen! I am making a promise to you, and to all your descendants,
and to every living creature with you: the birds, the cattle, and the wild animals, all that left the ark.
This is my promise to you: no flood will ever again wipe out all living things, and none will ever again destroy the earth.”
God continued, “I am giving you a sign of the promise I make to you, to every living creature with you, and to all the people who will ever live.
My bow{f} now rests in the clouds, a sign of my promise to the earth.
Whenever I gather clouds over the earth and the bow shows in them,
I will remember the promise I made to you and to every living creature. Floodwaters will never again destroy all life.
When the bow shows in the clouds, I will see it and remember my promise that lasts forever,{g} between God and all living creatures on the earth.”
God told Noah, “That bow is the sign of the promise I have made with all life on the earth.”
The sons of Noah who left the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. (Ham was Canaan’s father.)
From these three sons of Noah, all the peoples of the earth descended.{h}
Noah farmed the soil, and he planted the first vineyard.{i}
He drank a lot of the wine and passed out, lying uncovered inside his tent.
Ham, Canaan’s father, saw that his father was uncovered.{j} He ran to tell his two brothers.
Shem and Japheth lifted a robe onto their shoulders. Walking backward, they entered the tent and draped it over their father. They looked away the whole time and did not see him uncovered.
When Noah slept off his wine and learned what his youngest son{k} had done to him,
he said, “Cursed be Canaan!{l} He will be the lowest of servants{m} to his brothers.”
He added, “Praise Yahweh, the God of Shem!{n} May Canaan serve Shem.
May God make Japheth’s land wide.{o} May Japheth share the tents of Shem,{p} and may Canaan serve him too.”
After the flood, Noah lived another 350 years.
Noah died at the age of 950.

notes.text: Literally “flesh with its life, its blood.” Blood stands for life, and life belongs to God (see Leviticus 17:11).
Hebrew darash, “seek” or “demand.”
Literally “from the hand of each man, his brother, I will demand the life of the human.”
The Hebrew is a mirror of sounds: “sheds blood of the human, by the human his blood is shed.”
The Septuagint says “fill the earth and rule over it.”
Hebrew qeshet, the ordinary word for a war bow. God may be hanging up his weapon.
Hebrew berit olam, “lasting promise” or “everlasting covenant.”
Literally “spread out,” which looks ahead to the scattering in 11:8–9.
Literally “Noah, a man of the ground, began and planted a vineyard.”
What Ham did is debated. Some think it was more than looking, because “uncovering the nakedness” of a father may name a serious wrong.
Hebrew qatan, “small,” so “younger” or “youngest.” Ham is usually listed second.
The curse falls on Canaan, not on Ham. It looks ahead to Israel’s later fights with the Canaanites.
A Hebrew superlative, “a slave of slaves.”
Noah blesses Shem’s God instead of blessing Shem. Shem means “name,” and the God of Shem is Yahweh.
Hebrew yaft, “make wide,” sounds like Yefet, Japheth. The Septuagint says “make room for.”
“He” may be Japheth, or God living among the families of Shem.

verses.text: These are the families of Noah’s sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. They had children after the flood.
Japheth’s sons:{a} Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.
Gomer’s sons: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.
Javan’s sons: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.{b}
From these came the peoples of the coasts and islands.{c} Each group spread out into its own land, with its own language, clans, and nations.
Ham’s sons: Cush, Mizraim,{d} Put, and Canaan.
Cush’s sons: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. Raamah’s sons: Sheba and Dedan.
Cush was also the father of Nimrod.{e} He grew into the first great warrior on earth.
He was a mighty hunter in the sight of Yahweh.{f} That is why people say, “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before Yahweh.”
His kingdom began with the cities of Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh,{g} in the land of Shinar.{h}
From there he went into Assyria{i} and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-ir,{j} and Calah,
and also Resen, the big city between Nineveh and Calah.
Mizraim was the ancestor of the Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim,
Pathrusim, Casluhim (the ancestors of the Philistines),{k} and Caphtorim.
Canaan’s oldest son was Sidon. Canaan was also the ancestor of Heth,{l}
and of the Jebusites, Amorites, Girgashites,
Hivites, Arkites, Sinites,
Arvadites, Zemarites, and Hamathites. Later the Canaanite clans spread out.
The Canaanite border ran from Sidon toward Gerar as far as Gaza, then toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.
Those are the sons of Ham, listed by clan, language, land, and nation.
Children were also born to Shem. He was the ancestor of all the sons of Eber,{m} and the older brother of Japheth.{n}
Shem’s sons: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram.{o}
Aram’s sons: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.{p}
Arpachshad was the father of Shelah,{q} and Shelah was the father of Eber.
Eber had two sons. One was named Peleg,{r} because the earth was divided during his lifetime. His brother was named Joktan.
Joktan’s sons: Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,
Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,
Obal, Abimael, Sheba,
Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All of these were Joktan’s sons.
Their land stretched from Mesha toward Sephar, in the eastern hills.
Those are the sons of Shem, listed by clan, language, land, and nation.
These are the clans of Noah’s sons, family by family and nation by nation. After the flood, all the peoples of the earth branched out from them.{s}

notes.text: Many names in this chapter are of peoples and places as well as men. Gomer is often linked with the Cimmerians.
The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and 1 Chronicles 1:7 say Rodanim, the people of Rhodes.
Literally “the coastlands of the nations,” the shores and islands of the Mediterranean Sea.
Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt. Cush is the land south of Egypt. Put is probably Libya.
Nimrod sounds like the Hebrew for “we will rebel.”
“Before Yahweh” may mean “in Yahweh’s sight,” as a sign of greatness, or “against Yahweh.”
With other vowels, “and Calneh” can mean “all of them”: “Babel, Erech, and Accad, all of them.”
Shinar is Babylonia, in southern Mesopotamia.
Or “From that land Asshur went out.”
Literally “the broad places of the city,” perhaps a part of Nineveh.
Many scholars think this comment belongs after “Caphtorim,” since other books say the Philistines came from Caphtor (Amos 9:7).
Heth is the ancestor of the Hittites (see Genesis 23).
The name Eber is linked with the word “Hebrew.”
Or “the brother of Japheth the elder.” The Hebrew does not say which brother was older.
The Septuagint adds Cainan to the sons of Shem.
1 Chronicles 1:17 and the Septuagint read Meshech.
The Septuagint says Arpachshad was the father of Cainan, and Cainan of Shelah, as in Luke 3:36.
Peleg means “division.” The division may be the scattering in 11:1–9.
The Hebrew text names seventy peoples, a number that stands for completeness. With the Septuagint’s additions it is seventy-two.

verses.text: At one time the whole world spoke a single language, using the same words.{a}
As they moved along from the east,{b} they found a flat valley in the land of Shinar and stayed there.
They told each other, “Come on, let’s shape bricks and fire them until they are hard.”{c} For building they used brick instead of stone, and tar instead of mortar.
“Next,” they said, “we will put up a city for ourselves, with a tower whose top touches the heavens. We will win a name{d} for ourselves; otherwise we will be spread across the world.”
Yahweh came down to inspect the city and the tower being built by humans.{e}
He said, “Look! One people, one language, and this is just where they start. From here on, nothing they plan will be beyond their reach.
Come, let’s go down and scramble their speech{f} so they cannot follow one another’s words.”
So from that spot Yahweh scattered them across the entire earth, and the city was left unfinished.
This is how it got the name Babel:{g} Yahweh scrambled the world’s one language there, and from there he spread the people everywhere.
This is the family record of Shem.{h} Two years after the flood, when Shem was 100 years old, Arpachshad became his son.
For 500 years afterward Shem kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.{i}
Arpachshad was 35 years old when Shelah{j} became his son.
For 403 years afterward Arpachshad kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Shelah was 30 years old when Eber became his son.
For 403 years afterward Shelah kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Eber was 34 years old when Peleg became his son.
For 430 years afterward Eber kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Peleg was 30 years old when Reu became his son.
For 209 years afterward Peleg kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Reu was 32 years old when Serug became his son.
For 207 years afterward Reu kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Serug was 30 years old when Nahor became his son.
For 200 years afterward Serug kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
Nahor was 29 years old when Terah became his son.
For 119 years afterward Nahor kept on living and fathering sons and daughters.
When Terah was 70 years old, he became the father of Abram,{k} Nahor, and Haran.
Here is the family record of Terah. Terah had three sons: Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran had a son, Lot.
Haran died in the land where he was born, Ur of the Chaldeans,{l} while Terah, his father, was still living.
Abram and Nahor each took a wife. Abram’s wife was Sarai.{m} Nahor’s wife was Milcah, a daughter of Haran. (Haran had another daughter, Iscah.)
Sarai had no children, because she could not.{n}

Terah set out with his son Abram, Abram’s wife Sarai (Terah’s daughter-in-law), and his grandson Lot, the son of Haran. Together{o} they left Ur of the Chaldeans, headed for Canaan. On reaching Haran,{p} however, they made it their home.
Terah lived 205 years,{q} and he died in Haran.

notes.text: Literally “one lip and the same words.”
Or “traveled eastward.” In these early chapters people keep moving east, away from Eden (3:24; 4:16).
The Hebrew plays with sounds: “let us brick bricks and burn them for burning.”
Hebrew shem, “name.” In 12:2 God promises to make Abram’s name great.
The tower was so small, compared with the sky, that Yahweh had to “come down” to see it.
Literally “their lip.”
Babel is the Hebrew name for Babylon. It sounds like balal, “mix up.”
Hebrew toledot, “family record.” Ten generations from Shem to Abram match the ten from Adam to Noah in chapter 5.
The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint add “and he died” after each person in this list. The Septuagint also has different ages.
The Septuagint adds another person here: Arpachshad fathers Cainan, and Cainan fathers Shelah.
Abram means “exalted father.” In 17:5 he is renamed Abraham. He is listed first, but he may not be the oldest.
Ur was a great city in southern Mesopotamia. “Of the Chaldeans” is a later name for the region.
Sarai probably means “princess.” In 17:15 she is renamed Sarah.
Literally “barren; she had no child.” This short sentence sets up the story of the promise that follows.
Literally “they went out with them.” The Septuagint and Vulgate read “he brought them out.”
The city of Haran in northern Mesopotamia is spelled differently in Hebrew from the man Haran.
The Samaritan Pentateuch says 145 years.

verses.text: Yahweh said to Abram: “Pack up and walk away{a} from your homeland, from your extended family, and from the house where your father lives. I will lead you to a country that I will show you.
There I will build your family into a mighty nation. I will favor you, give you a famous name, and make you a blessing to others.{b}
Those who wish you well will find me wishing them well. Those who treat you with scorn will find a curse waiting for them. Every family{c} on earth will find blessing through you.”{d}
So Abram set out, just as Yahweh had said. His nephew Lot{e} traveled with him. Abram had reached the age of 75 by the time he left Haran.

With him went his wife Sarai, Lot, every possession they had collected, and the people{f} they had taken into their household while living in Haran. Together they started for Canaan, and they got there.
Abram crossed the country to Shechem, where the big tree of Moreh{g} stands. In those days Canaanites lived throughout the region.
Yahweh showed himself to Abram and promised, “I will hand this country over to your descendants.”{h} There Abram put up an altar to honor Yahweh, who had shown himself to him.

From there Abram climbed into the hill country on the eastern side of Bethel and pitched his tent. Bethel lay to the west of his camp and Ai to the east. He built an altar to Yahweh in that place and worshiped, calling on Yahweh by name.
After that he kept moving in stages toward the Negev,{i} in the south.
Food ran short in the land because of a famine. So Abram traveled down to Egypt and stayed there as a guest from another country.{j}
Just before they crossed into Egypt, Abram spoke to Sarai. “You are lovely to look at, and I know it.
Egyptians will notice you and think, ‘She must be his wife.’ They will then put me to death and keep you alive.
So say you are my sister.{k} That way I will be treated kindly because of you, and my life will be spared.”
Once Abram was in Egypt, the Egyptians could not help noticing how lovely Sarai was.
Officials{l} who worked for Pharaoh saw her and described her to him in glowing words. She was brought into the royal palace.
For her sake the king gave Abram gifts: sheep, cattle, male donkeys, female donkeys, camels,{m} and male and female servants.
Yahweh, though, sent harsh illnesses on Pharaoh and everyone in his house, since Sarai was Abram’s wife.
Pharaoh called Abram in. “Look at what you did to me! Why would you not tell me she was your wife?
Why did you let me think she was your sister, so that I made her my wife? She is yours again. Take her and leave!”
Pharaoh told his soldiers what to do. They led Abram out of Egypt with his wife and all of his belongings.

notes.text: Hebrew lekh-lekha, “go for yourself.” The same words open the test in 22:2, so Abraham’s story is framed by two calls to go.
Or “you will be a blessing.” Some scholars read the Hebrew as “your name will be a blessing.”
Or “clan.” The Septuagint says “tribe.”

Or “will bless themselves by you,” that is, use your name when they bless each other. The New Testament reads it as a promise that the nations will share Abraham’s blessing (Acts 3:25; Galatians 3:8).
Lot probably means “covering” (meaning uncertain). He was the son of Abram’s brother Haran (11:27).
Literally “the souls.” The word means the servants and others who belonged to the household.
Or “the oak of Moreh.” Moreh may mean “teacher.” The Septuagint says “the high oak.”
Literally “seed,” here and later in Genesis. The Hebrew word is singular in form but usually means a whole family line.
The Negev is the dry southern part of Canaan. The word also means “south.”
Hebrew gur, “to live as a foreigner without the rights of a native.”
Sarai was really Abram’s half sister (20:12). Still, the half-truth was meant to fool people, and the story does not praise it.
Or “princes.” “Pharaoh” is the Egyptian title for the king. It means “great house.”
Some scholars question camels this early. The writer may have used a detail familiar to later readers.

verses.text: Abram traveled north from Egypt into the Negev. He took his wife, all his goods, and Lot.
Abram had become a very rich man.{a} He owned huge numbers of animals, and he had silver and gold.
He moved from place to place, going from the Negev up to Bethel, and finally reached the spot between Bethel and Ai where his tent had stood earlier.
It was the same spot where he had put up his first altar. Abram worshiped Yahweh there once more.
Lot, Abram’s traveling partner, had sheep, cattle, and tents too.
There was not enough grazing land for both of them to live side by side. Together they had so much livestock that the land could not hold them.
The men who tended Abram’s animals began quarreling with the men who tended Lot’s animals. Canaanites and Perizzites lived in that land too at the time.
Abram went to Lot with a suggestion. “We are family,{b} so there should be no fighting between us or between the men who work for us.
Look, you can pick any part of the country. Let’s divide it. Go left, and I will go right. Go right, and I will go left.”

Lot gazed around. The whole Jordan Valley{c} was green and well watered, as far as Zoar.{d} It resembled Yahweh’s own garden, and also the land of Egypt. (Yahweh had not yet ruined Sodom and Gomorrah at that time.)
Lot picked for himself all of the Jordan Valley and traveled east. The two relatives went their own ways.
Abram remained in Canaan. Lot made his home among the valley towns, moving his tent as far as the edge of Sodom.
Sodom’s people were bad. They committed terrible sins against Yahweh.{e}
After Lot left, Yahweh spoke to Abram: “Lift your eyes from this spot and gaze in every direction, north, south, east, and west.{f}
I am giving you every bit of ground you can see, and your descendants will keep it forever.
Your descendants will be like dust, too many to count. You might as well try to count the grains of dust on the earth.
Now go and walk across this land, from end to end and side to side. It is going to be yours.”
Abram packed up his tents and settled near the great trees of Mamre,{g} by Hebron. He built an altar there to honor Yahweh.

notes.text: Literally “very heavy.” The same Hebrew root gives the word for “glory.”
Literally “for we are men, brothers.” “Brother” can mean any close relative. Lot was Abram’s nephew.
Hebrew kikkar, “circle” or “round.” It names the well-watered region around the southern Jordan.
Zoar means “small place” (see 19:22). Its older name was Bela (14:2). The Septuagint says “Zogora.”
Literally “evil and sinners to Yahweh, very much.” The Septuagint says “before God.”
Literally “seaward,” that is, toward the Mediterranean Sea.
Or “the terebinths of Mamre.” The Hebrew is plural, and the Septuagint has the singular “oak.”

verses.text: A war once broke out in the days of four kings: Amraphel, ruler of Shinar; Arioch, ruler of Ellasar; Chedorlaomer, ruler of Elam; and Tidal, ruler of Goiim.{a}

They fought against five other rulers. These were Bera, who ruled Sodom; Birsha, who ruled Gomorrah; Shinab, the ruler of Admah; Shemeber, the ruler of Zeboiim; and the king of Bela, a town also called Zoar.
The five allies brought all their armies to the Valley of Siddim, which is now covered by the Dead Sea.{b}
These five had been under Chedorlaomer’s rule for twelve years, but in year thirteen they turned against him.
In year fourteen, Chedorlaomer came with the kings on his side. Along the way they defeated the Rephaim{c} at Ashteroth-karnaim. They also beat the Zuzim at Ham, and the Emim at Shaveh-kiriathaim.
They also beat the Horites, who lived in the hills of Seir, and chased them all the way to El-paran, beside the desert.
Then the army swung around and marched to En-mishpat{d} (another name for Kadesh). There they took over the land of the Amalekites, and the land of the Amorites at Hazazon-tamar too.
At that point the five kings of the valley cities, Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela (which is Zoar), moved their troops into place in the Valley of Siddim.
Chedorlaomer of Elam was joined by the kings of Goiim, Shinar, and Ellasar (Tidal, Amraphel, and Arioch). Four kings stood against five.
Siddim was a valley full of tar pits.{e} As the armies of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, many men tumbled into the pits. The survivors ran into the hills.
The victors collected all the wealth and food of Sodom and Gomorrah and marched off.
Lot, Abram’s nephew, lived in Sodom, so they took him along with everything he owned.

A man who had gotten away reached Abram the Hebrew{f} with the news. At that time Abram was camping among the big trees of Mamre the Amorite. Mamre had two brothers, Eshcol and Aner, and all three had made an agreement to help Abram.{g}
Abram heard that his nephew was a prisoner. He summoned{h} the 318 men he had trained, who had all been born into his household, and pursued the raiders as far north as Dan.{i}
Under cover of night he divided his men into squads, and they struck the enemy together with Abram’s servants. The enemy broke, and Abram drove them past Damascus, up to Hobah on its north side.{j}
He recovered everything that had been stolen. He also freed his nephew Lot and got back Lot’s property, along with the women and the rest of the prisoners.
When Abram came back after beating Chedorlaomer and his allies, the king of Sodom walked out to greet him at the Valley of Shaveh. People call it the King’s Valley.
Melchizedek,{k} who ruled Salem{l} and served as a priest of El Elyon,{m} came out with gifts of bread and wine.
He spoke a blessing over Abram: “Abram, may El Elyon, the maker{n} of heaven and earth, bless you.
Praise El Elyon for handing your enemies over to you!” In return, Abram gave Melchizedek one tenth of everything he had won back.{o}
Then the king of Sodom made an offer. “Let me have the people. Keep all the goods yourself.”
Abram replied, “I have sworn{p} to Yahweh,{q} El Elyon, creator of heaven and earth,
that nothing of yours will stay with me, not even a single thread or shoelace. You will never be able to say, ‘Abram got rich thanks to me.’
I will take only the food my young men ate. My allies Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre should take their portion, since they came with me.”

notes.text: Goiim may mean “nations,” as the Septuagint reads. None of these four kings is clearly known from other ancient records.
Hebrew “the Salt Sea.” The notes “that is...” in this chapter give readers the later name for old places.
The Rephaim, Zuzim, and Emim were peoples remembered as very tall (compare Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 20). The Septuagint says “the giants” for Rephaim.
En-mishpat means “spring of judgment.”
Literally “pits, pits of bitumen,” which means “full of tar pits.” Natural tar is common around the Dead Sea.
This is the first time “Hebrew” appears in the Bible. The Septuagint says “the one who crossed over.” The word may instead come from Abram’s ancestor Eber (10:21; 11:14).
Literally “lords of an agreement with Abram.”
Literally “emptied out.” Most likely it means “called out for battle.” The Septuagint says “counted.”
Dan got that name later (Judges 18:29). The writer uses the name his readers knew.
Literally “on the left of,” which is north for a person facing east.
Melchizedek means “my king is right” or “king of what is right.” Psalm 110:4, Hebrews 5-7, and a Dead Sea Scroll about Melchizedek all refer to him.
Salem is probably Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2). It sounds like shalom, “peace.”
Hebrew El Elyon means “God Most High.” Elyon means “highest.” In 14:22 Abram says this God is Yahweh.
Or “owns” or “created.” The Hebrew qoneh can mean “maker” or “owner.”
Literally “he gave him a tenth from all.” The Hebrew does not say who gave. Hebrews 7:4 understands that Abram gave it to Melchizedek.
Literally “raised my hand,” a gesture for taking an oath. The Septuagint says “I will stretch out my hand.”
The Hebrew text names Yahweh here, and the Septuagint says “the Lord.” Some other ancient witnesses are reported to have only “God Most High” (El Elyon), as in 14:18-20.

verses.text: Later, Yahweh gave Abram a message in a vision: “Do not be afraid, Abram. I will guard you like a shield.{a} You will receive a very rich reward.”
Abram answered, “Lord Yahweh,{b} what good is any gift to me? I have no children. My house will go to Eliezer of Damascus.{c}
You never gave me a child, so the heir will be a man who works in my home.”
Yahweh replied, “No, he will not be your heir. Your own child will inherit from you.”
Then Yahweh took Abram outdoors. “Tilt your head back and look at the stars,” he said. “Can you number them? Your family will grow to be just that large.”
Abram put his trust{d} in Yahweh, and Yahweh took it as a sign that Abram was right with him.{e}
Yahweh continued, “I am the same Yahweh who brought you away from Ur of the Chaldeans. My purpose was to make this country yours.”
Abram said, “Lord Yahweh, what will show me that I really will get it?”
Yahweh answered, “Bring me a heifer, a female goat, and a ram. Each must be three years old. Bring a dove and a young pigeon too.”
Abram collected them all. He cut each of the larger animals down the middle and placed the two halves across from one another. The birds he left in one piece.
Meat-eating birds came flying down to the bodies, but Abram waved them off.{f}
At sunset Abram fell into a heavy sleep,{g} and a thick, frightening darkness settled over him.

Then Yahweh spoke: “Know this for certain. Your descendants will live as strangers in a country that does not belong to them. They will serve the people of that country as slaves and suffer harsh treatment for 400 years.{h}
I will judge that country and its rulers. After that your people will walk out with great riches.
You yourself will go to your ancestors in peace. You will be laid in the grave after a long life.
Your descendants will come back here in the fourth generation.{i} The wrongdoing of the Amorites has not yet grown big enough for me to act.”
After sunset, in the dark, a smoking fire pot and a burning torch drifted between the halves of the animals.{j}
That same day Yahweh entered into an agreement{k} with Abram, saying, “I give this land to your descendants. It reaches from the river of Egypt{l} to the great river Euphrates.
It includes the territory of the Kenites, Kenizzites, and Kadmonites,
and of the Hittites, Perizzites, and Rephaim,
and of the Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites, and Jebusites.”{m}

notes.text: Hebrew magen, “shield.” Changing a few vowels gives “I give you a gift,” which some scholars like because of the word “reward.” The Septuagint says “I shield you.”
Hebrew Adonai Yahweh, “my Lord Yahweh.” Older English Bibles print “Lord GOD.” The Septuagint says “Master and Lord.”
The Hebrew is hard to read. Literally it says “the son of mesheq of my house is Damascus Eliezer.” Mesheq may be a play on the sound of Dammesheq, “Damascus.”
Or “believed.” The Hebrew he’emin comes from the same root as “amen,” which means “firm” or “reliable.” Romans 4:3, Galatians 3:6, and James 2:23 quote this verse.
The Hebrew does not say who “counted” it. Most readers think Yahweh counted Abram’s trust as being right with him. A few think Abram counted Yahweh’s promise as a fair and right one.
The Septuagint says “Abram sat down by them.”
Hebrew tardemah, the same deep sleep that came on the first man in 2:21. The Septuagint says “a trance.”

Exodus 12:40 says 430 years. The Septuagint and, reportedly, the Samaritan Pentateuch count that time as including the years in Canaan before Egypt. Paul counts 430 years from the promise to the Law (Galatians 3:17).
Hebrew dor, “generation,” may here mean a long span of about 100 years, to match the 400 years in verse 13.

In ancient agreements the people walked between cut animals, calling the same fate on themselves if they broke their word (compare Jeremiah 34:18-20). Here only the fire, a sign of God, passes between.
Hebrew berit, “covenant.” The Hebrew says “cut a covenant,” which fits the cut animals.
Probably the Wadi el-Arish, a stream that flows only in the rainy season on the border of Egypt, not the Nile.
The Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses add “the Hivites.” This Bible follows the Hebrew, which names ten peoples.

verses.text: Sarai, Abram’s wife, was unable to have a child for him. She did own a servant from Egypt, a woman called Hagar.{a}
Sarai told Abram, “Yahweh has stopped me from having babies. Take my servant as your partner. Perhaps a child born to her can become mine.”{b} Abram did as Sarai urged.
Ten years had gone by since Abram settled in Canaan. Then Sarai took Hagar, her Egyptian servant, and gave her to Abram to be his wife.{c}
Abram lay with Hagar, and she soon expected a baby. When Hagar saw that, she started treating her mistress Sarai with scorn.{d}
Sarai complained to Abram: “You are to blame for this wrong against me! I put my servant in your arms. Now she is expecting, and she looks down on me. Let Yahweh be the judge between us.”{e}
“Your servant is under your control,” Abram said. “Handle it however you think best.” So Sarai made life so hard{f} for Hagar that Hagar fled.
In the desert, beside the spring along the Shur road, the angel of Yahweh{g} came upon Hagar.
“Hagar, Sarai’s servant,” he asked, “where did you come from? Where are you going?” “I am escaping from Sarai, my mistress,” she said.
The angel of Yahweh told her, “Return to Sarai and accept her authority.”
He continued, “Your descendants will be so many that nobody could ever count them.”
Then the angel of Yahweh said, “You are expecting a boy. Name him Ishmael,{h} for Yahweh has listened to your cries of pain.
He will live free like a wild donkey.{i} He will quarrel with everyone, and everyone will quarrel with him. He will make his home alongside{j} his relatives, always in conflict with them.
Hagar gave a title to Yahweh, who had spoken with her. She called him El Roi.{k} She wondered, “Have I truly caught sight of the One who sees me, and lived?”{l}
For this reason people call that well Beer-lahai-roi.{m} You can find it between Kadesh and Bered.
Hagar bore a son to Abram, and Abram gave the boy the name Ishmael.
Abram’s age when Ishmael was born to Hagar was 86.

notes.text: Hagar probably means “flight” or “stranger” (meaning uncertain). The Hebrew word for “servant” here means a woman who belonged to her mistress.
Literally “I will be built from her.” The Hebrew plays on banah, “build,” and ben, “son.”
Or “as a secondary wife.” Hagar was now a wife, but she was still Sarai’s servant (16:6).
Literally “her mistress became light in her eyes,” the opposite of honored.
Literally “May Yahweh judge between me and you.” Sarai’s first words, “my violence is on you,” mean “you are responsible for the wrong done to me.”
Hebrew anah, “to humble” or “to hurt.” The same word is used for Israel’s suffering in Egypt (15:13; Exodus 1:11-12).
This is the first time “the angel (or messenger) of Yahweh” appears. In several passages he speaks as God himself (16:10, 13; 22:11-12, 15-16).
Ishmael means “God hears.”
Hebrew pere, the wild donkey of the desert. It pictures a free, untamed life, not an insult. The Septuagint says “a wild man.”
Or “live to the east of” or “live beside.” The Hebrew al-pene, “on the face of,” can mean any of these. The Septuagint says “in front of.”
Hebrew El Roi means “the God who sees me.”
The Hebrew is hard to read. A literal rendering is “Have I even here seen after the one who sees me?” It may mean “Have I seen God and lived after seeing him?”
Beer-lahai-roi probably means “well of the Living One who looks on me.”

verses.text: When Abram reached 99, Yahweh showed himself to him again. “I am El Shaddai,”{a} Yahweh said. “Live your life in my sight, with honesty and no blame.{b}
Then I will make my agreement with you and make your family grow very large.”
Abram dropped to the ground, face down. God continued:
“Here is what I promise you. You will become the father of a crowd of nations.
Your name will no longer be Abram. From now on you will be Abraham,{c} since I have made you the father of a crowd of nations.
I will make you wonderfully fruitful. Whole nations will grow from you, and some of your descendants will be kings.
I will make an unending agreement between me and you and all your later generations. You and your descendants will have me as your God.
The country where you now live as a foreigner, all of Canaan, I will give to you and your descendants as a permanent possession. I will be their God.”
God said to Abraham, “You, for your part, must hold to my agreement, you and each generation that follows you.
Here is what you must do to hold to it: every male in your group will be circumcised.
You will cut off the foreskin. That mark will show that you belong to my agreement.
From now on, every boy will be circumcised on his eighth day of life. This applies to boys born in your household and to slaves you buy from outsiders who are not of your family.
Boys born in your home and slaves bought with your money all need this. Then my agreement will be in your bodies as a lasting sign.
A male who refuses to be circumcised{d} will be removed{e} from his people, since he has broken my agreement.”
God spoke to Abraham again: “As for your wife Sarai, stop calling her that. Her name is Sarah{f} now.
I will bless her, and through her I will give you a son. Yes, I will bless her, and she will be the mother of nations. Kings of peoples will be born from her.”{g}
Abraham fell face down again, and he laughed.{h} Inside he wondered, “Will a man who is 100 become a father? Will Sarah give birth at 90?”
Abraham said to God, “I wish Ishmael could be the one who lives under your blessing.”
“No,” God said.{i} “Your wife Sarah will bear you a son. Name him Isaac.{j} My agreement will stand with him, and it will last forever with his descendants.

About Ishmael, I have heard your request.{k} I will bless him. I will make his family large and give him many descendants. Twelve princes will come from him, and I will turn his descendants into a great nation.
My agreement, though, I will keep with Isaac. Sarah will have him for you at this time next year.”
God finished talking with Abraham and went up and away from him.
Abraham acted on that very day. He gathered his son Ishmael and every male in his household, both those born there and those he had bought, and circumcised them just as God had instructed.
Abraham was 99 at the time of his own circumcision,
and Ishmael was 13.
On that very day Abraham and his son Ishmael both went through it,
along with every other man in the house, whether home-born or bought from outsiders.

notes.text: Hebrew El Shaddai is often rendered “God Almighty.” The meaning of Shaddai is uncertain. Suggestions include “of the mountain,” “of the fields,” and “the one who is enough.” The Septuagint here says “I am your God.”
Hebrew tamim, “whole” or “complete.” It is also used of Noah in 6:9.
Abram means “exalted father.” Abraham sounds like av hamon, “father of a crowd.” The new name gives the old one a new meaning.
The Septuagint adds “on the eighth day.” Some other ancient witnesses are reported to say the same.
“Cut off” (karat) may mean death, being sent away from the community, or the end of one’s family line. The same verb is used for “cutting” an agreement (15:18).
Sarai and Sarah are two forms of one name that means “princess.” The change marks her new place as the mother of nations and kings.
The Septuagint says “I will bless him, and he will become nations,” so that it talks about the son.
Hebrew tsachaq, “to laugh.” It is the root of the name Isaac. Laughter comes up again in 18:12-15 and 21:6, 9.
Or “Truly” or “Yes, indeed.” The Hebrew aval can either agree or correct. The Septuagint says “Yes.”
Isaac (Hebrew Yitschaq) means “he laughs.”
Hebrew shema’tikha, “I have heard you,” which plays on the name Ishmael, “God hears.”

verses.text: Abraham was sitting in the doorway of his tent beside the big trees of Mamre when Yahweh appeared to him. The sun was blazing hot.
When he glanced up, three men stood a short way off. He jumped up, hurried over, and bent low to the ground in front of them.
“Sir,{a} if I have your good opinion, please do not walk past your servant.
Let me send for water so you can wash your dusty feet and then rest in the shade of the tree.
I will fetch a bite to eat, so you can regain your strength before moving on. That is why you came by my tent, after all.” They agreed: “Do what you have offered.”
Abraham dashed into the tent and told Sarah, “Quick! Take about 20 quarts{b} of fine flour, make dough, and bake bread.”
He himself sprinted to the cattle, selected a tender, healthy calf, and handed it to a young servant, who rushed to prepare it.
Abraham served them yogurt,{c} milk, and the roasted calf. While they ate, he waited on them, standing beneath the tree.
“Where is your wife Sarah?” the men asked. “She is in the tent,” he said.
Then one said, “In about a year I will visit you again, and Sarah will be holding a baby boy.”{d} Sarah heard this from the tent entrance behind him.
Both Abraham and Sarah were very old, and Sarah was too old to bear children.
She chuckled to herself. “I am worn out and my husband is old, so how could I have joy now?”{e} she thought.
Yahweh said to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh and say, ‘Could I truly have a baby at my age?’
Does Yahweh find anything impossible?{f} I will come back to you at the proper time, a year from now, and Sarah will hold a son in her arms.
Sarah was frightened and denied it. “I did not laugh.” “Oh yes, you did,” he said.
The men rose and gazed toward Sodom. Abraham accompanied them part of the way.
Yahweh thought, “Should I keep Abraham in the dark about my plans?
He is going to father a great, strong nation, and all the nations of the earth will receive blessing through him.
I picked him{g} to teach his children and his household to follow Yahweh’s path, doing what is good and fair. Then Yahweh can give Abraham what he promised.”
Yahweh said, “A huge outcry rises against Sodom and Gomorrah, and their sin is very serious.
I am going down to check whether they truly do what the outcry says. If not, I will find that out.”
The men went toward Sodom. Abraham remained where he was, in front of Yahweh.{h}
He came forward and said, “Would you really wipe out innocent people together with guilty people?
Imagine fifty innocent people in the city. Would you still wipe it out? Would you not forgive the whole place for those fifty?
It cannot be that you would kill the innocent along with the guilty and treat them alike. That is unthinkable! Will the Judge of all the earth not be fair?”
Yahweh said, “If fifty innocent people live in Sodom, I will forgive the whole city for their sake.”
Abraham answered, “I know I am just dust and ashes,{i} but let me speak to the Lord once more.
Perhaps the fifty will lack five. Will you wipe out the whole city for want of five?” Yahweh said, “If I find 45 there, I will spare it.”
Abraham pressed on. “Perhaps only 40.” Yahweh said, “I will hold back for 40.”
“Lord, please do not be angry,” Abraham said, “but let me ask. Perhaps only 30.” Yahweh said, “I will hold back if I find 30 there.”
Abraham said, “I am daring to speak to the Lord again. Perhaps only 20.” Yahweh said, “I will not destroy it, for 20’s sake.”
He said, “Lord, please do not be angry. I will ask only this one last time. Perhaps only ten.” Yahweh said, “Because of ten, I will not destroy it.”
After Yahweh finished speaking with Abraham, he departed, and Abraham returned to his tent.

notes.text: Or “My lord.” The Hebrew letters can be read as adoni, “my lord,” a polite way to address a guest, or as Adonai, “Lord.” Abraham may not yet know who his visitor is.

Hebrew “three seahs.” A seah was a dry measure of uncertain size, often figured at about 7 quarts (7.3 liters). Three seahs is about 20 quarts (22 liters). Some estimates are much smaller. Either way it is a huge amount for three guests.
Or “butter.” Hebrew chem’ah usually means thick, soured milk like yogurt.
Literally “at the time of life,” that is, when the season comes around again.
Hebrew ednah, a word related to Eden, “delight.”
Or “too wonderful for Yahweh?” Hebrew pala is used for things beyond human power. Compare Jeremiah 32:17, 27 and Luke 1:37.
Literally “I have known him,” meaning a close, chosen relationship.
Jewish scribes listed this verse among their “corrections.” They said it first read “Yahweh stood in front of Abraham,” and it was changed out of respect. No copy that survives has that wording.
Hebrew aphar wa’epher, a pair of words that sound alike. Compare 3:19.

verses.text: The two angels reached Sodom at dusk. Lot happened to be sitting in the city gateway.{a} When Lot saw them, he got to his feet, went over to greet them, and knelt with his forehead touching the ground.
“Gentlemen,” he said, “I beg you to turn in at my house. Spend the night, wash your feet, and leave early tomorrow.” But they said, “No, we will sleep in the open square.”
He pressed them so hard that they finally gave in and went to his house. He had a meal made and baked flat bread, and they ate.
They had not yet gone to bed when every man in Sodom, young and old, closed in around the house.
They shouted to Lot, “Where are the men who came to stay with you tonight? Send them out here. We want to do what we like with them!”{b}
Lot stepped out the front door and pulled it closed.
“My friends, I beg you, do not commit this crime,” he said.

“I have two daughters who have never slept with anyone. I will send them out, and you may treat them any way you wish. Only leave these men alone. They have come under my roof,{c} and I must keep them safe.”

“Move aside!” they yelled. “You are a foreigner who moved in, and now you act like our judge!{d} We will hurt you more than we would hurt them.” They shoved Lot back and crowded forward to smash the door.
Inside, the visitors seized Lot, dragged him in, and bolted the door.
Then they blinded{e} the men outside, young and old, with a flash of light, and the crowd wore itself out hunting for the door.
The visitors asked Lot, “Is there anyone else of yours in this place? A son-in-law, sons, daughters, any relative in the city? Take them all out of here,
for we are going to wipe the city out. Yahweh has heard how loud the cry against it is, and he has sent us to destroy it.”
Lot hurried to the men who had promised to marry{f} his daughters. “Get up and leave this place at once,” he said. “Yahweh is about to destroy the city.” They took it as a joke.
At first light the angels rushed him. “Get moving! Your wife and the two daughters here with you must go now, or the city’s punishment{g} will sweep you away too.”
He still dragged his feet. Yahweh felt sorry for him, so the men grabbed Lot, his wife, and his two daughters by the hands and rushed them out, setting them outside the city walls.
Once they were out, one of them{h} told Lot, “Run, or you will die! Do not look behind you. Do not stop anywhere on the plain. Race for the mountains, or you will be wiped out.”
“Please, my lord, no!”{i} Lot said.
“You have shown me kindness and spared my life. But the mountains are too far. Before I reach them, the disaster will overtake me, and I will be dead.
Look, that little town over there is close enough to reach. It is tiny. Let me go there. It is such a small place that my life will be safe.”
“Very well,” the angel said. “I will do this favor for you too. I will leave that town standing.{j}
Go quickly! I can do nothing until you are inside it.” This is how the town got its name, Zoar.{k}
The sun was rising over the land as Lot entered Zoar.
Then Yahweh poured down fire and burning sulfur from the sky onto Sodom and Gomorrah. It came from Yahweh himself.{l}
He wiped out both cities and the entire plain, every person in the cities, and every plant that grew from the soil.
Lot’s wife was walking behind him. She turned to look back, and she became a column of salt.{m}
Early the next morning, Abraham walked to the spot where he had stood before Yahweh.
Looking toward Sodom, Gomorrah, and all the plain, he saw dark smoke climbing from the ground, like smoke from a huge oven.
When God wiped out the cities of the plain, he kept Abraham in mind. He took Lot out of the disaster that overturned the towns where Lot had lived.
Afraid to remain in Zoar, Lot moved up into the mountains with his two daughters and lived in a cave.
The older girl told her sister, “Our father is getting old, and no man is around{n} to marry us the way people do everywhere.
Let’s give our father wine until he is drunk. Then we will sleep with him and keep our family line alive through him.”
That night they gave him wine. The older daughter went into his room and lay with him. He was too drunk to know when she came or when she left.{o}
The next morning she told her sister, “I slept with Father last night. Let’s make him drunk again tonight. You go and sleep with him, so that our family line will survive through our father.”
They gave him wine again that night. The younger daughter went and slept with him, and again he was too drunk to know when she came or when she left.
So both of Lot’s daughters were expecting children by their own father.
The older daughter had a baby boy and called him Moab.{p} He became the ancestor of today’s Moabites.
The younger one also had a son, whom she named Ben-ammi.{q} He became the ancestor of today’s Ammonites.

notes.text: The city gate was where people did business, held court, and talked over town matters. Sitting there may show that Lot had some standing in the city.

Literally “so that we may know them.” “Know” here means sex, as in 4:1. The men wanted to rape strangers who were under a host’s care, a terrible break of the rules of welcome. Compare Judges 19:22-25.
Literally “they have come under the shadow of my roof beams.” The story reports Lot’s offer of his daughters without approving it.
Literally “and now he sets himself up to judge.”
Hebrew sanverim, a rare word found only here and in 2 Kings 6:18. It may mean sudden dazzling light or confused sight.
Or “who had married.” The Hebrew can mean either one. Verse 8 says the daughters had never been with a man, so they were probably engaged.
Hebrew awon, “wrongdoing,” which also means the punishment it brings. The Septuagint says “the wrongs of the city.”
The Hebrew says “he said.” The Septuagint and some other ancient versions say “they said.”
