Or “my Lord.” As in 18:3, the Hebrew vowels read “Lord” (Adonai), but the letters also allow “my lords.”
Literally “I have lifted up your face in this matter also,” an old saying for granting a request.
Zoar sounds like mits’ar, “a small thing” (19:20). Its earlier name was Bela (14:2).
Saying “Yahweh” twice is unusual. Some early Christian writers saw two persons here. Others think it is a Hebrew way of saying “from himself.”
Jesus mentions this in Luke 17:32. Salt formations near the Dead Sea gave rise to local stories about the pillar (Wisdom of Solomon 10:7).
Or “on the earth.” The daughters may have thought the whole world was gone.
In the Hebrew text, a scribal dot stands over one letter in the words “when she got up.” It is an old mark of doubt or comment, found in only a few places in the Torah.
Moab sounds like me’av, “from father.” The Septuagint adds “saying, ‘He is from my father.’”
Ben-ammi means “son of my relative” or “son of my people.” The Septuagint says Amman and adds “saying, ‘Son of my family.’”

verses.text: Abraham left that area and traveled toward the Negev. He settled between Kadesh and Shur, and later stayed for a time in Gerar as a foreigner.
Abraham told the people there that Sarah was his sister. Abimelech,{a} the king of Gerar, had Sarah brought to his palace.
That night God came to Abimelech in a dream with a warning: “The woman you took will cost you your life, because she is already married.”{b}
Abimelech had not touched her. “Lord,” he said, “will you kill people who have done no wrong?{c}
Abraham himself said she was his sister, and she said he was her brother. I did this with a clean heart and clean hands.”{d}
God said to him in the dream, “I know your heart was clean. In fact, I am the one who stopped you from sinning against me and from touching her.
Now give the woman back to Abraham. He is a prophet,{e} and when he prays for you, you will live. If you do not send her back, you and everyone who belongs to you will surely die.”
Abimelech got up early, called together all his servants, and reported everything. The men were deeply afraid.

Next the king summoned Abraham. “How could you treat us this way? What did I do to you to deserve this? You have brought a terrible guilt on me and on my kingdom. Nobody should do to another what you have done to me.”
Abimelech went on, “What made you do such a thing?”{f}
Abraham explained, “I told myself that nobody here fears God, and that they would murder me over my wife.
She truly is my sister as well. Her father is my father, but her mother is not my mother. Later she became my wife.
When God made me wander{g} from my father’s house, I asked her for one kindness. In every place we visit, she was to say I am her brother.”
Abimelech brought sheep, cattle, and servants, both men and women, and gave them to Abraham. He also returned his wife Sarah.
“Take a look at my land,” he said. “Settle wherever you please.”
He told Sarah, “I have given your brother about 25 pounds of silver.{h} Let it settle the matter for you with everyone around you, so that you are cleared of all blame.”{i}
Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his female servants. They were able to have children again.
Yahweh had made every woman in Abimelech’s household unable to bear children because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife.

notes.text: Abimelech means “my father is king.” It may be a royal title as well as a name (compare 26:1).
Literally “she is owned by an owner (ba’al),” that is, she has a husband.
Literally “a righteous nation.” Abimelech’s words echo Abraham’s plea for Sodom (18:23-25). The Septuagint says “a nation that sins without knowing it, and is righteous.”
Literally “in the integrity of my heart and the cleanness of my palms.”
This is the first use of “prophet” (navi) in the Bible. Here the prophet’s job is to pray for others.
Literally “What did you see?”
The Hebrew verb is plural, so it could be read “the gods made me wander.” But Elohim, “God,” is sometimes used with plural verbs, and Abraham may be speaking so that a foreign king would understand.
Hebrew “a thousand of silver,” that is, 1,000 shekels. At about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams) each, that is about 25 pounds (11.5 kilograms). Weight standards varied.

Literally “let it be a covering of the eyes for you.” The saying is uncertain. It probably means the payment clears Sarah’s name so that others look away from the matter. The Septuagint says “the price of your face (your honor).”

verses.text: Yahweh looked after Sarah{a} and did for her exactly what he had promised.
Sarah became pregnant. In Abraham’s old age she gave birth to a son, right on the day God had named.
Abraham gave the name Isaac to the baby that Sarah had borne him.
When Isaac was eight days old, Abraham circumcised him, as God had ordered.
Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac arrived.
“Laughter has come to me from God,” Sarah said. “Everyone who hears the news will laugh together with me.”{b}
“Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would feed a baby at her breast?” she asked. “But now I have given him a son, and he is an old man.”
The child grew and was weaned. On the day of the weaning, Abraham held a big banquet.
One day Sarah saw Hagar’s son, the boy the Egyptian woman had borne to Abraham. He was laughing and playing.{c}
She told Abraham, “Send away that servant woman and her son! A servant’s boy will never share the family property with my son Isaac.”
This request hurt Abraham badly, since Ishmael was his own child.
But God told Abraham, “Do not let this trouble you, either about the boy or about your servant. Listen to Sarah and do whatever she says. Your family line will be counted through Isaac.{d}
I will make a nation out of the servant’s son as well, because he is your child too.”
Early the next morning Abraham took some bread and a skin full of water. He set them on Hagar’s shoulder, along with the boy,{e} and sent her away. She wandered through the desert near Beersheba.
When the water in the skin was gone, she pushed the boy under a bush.
She walked away and sat down by herself, a good bowshot from him. “I cannot stand to see my boy die,” she said. Sitting there, she began to cry loudly.{f}
God listened to the boy’s cries. From the sky the angel of God spoke to Hagar: “What is troubling you, Hagar? Fear nothing! God has heard the boy’s voice from where he is lying.
Get up, lift the child, and take his hand firmly. I am going to turn his family into a mighty nation.”
God opened her eyes, and a well came into view. She hurried over, filled the skin, and let the boy drink.
God was with the boy while he grew up. Ishmael settled in the wilderness and became a skilled archer.{g}
He settled in the Desert of Paran, and his mother found him a wife from Egypt.
About then, Abimelech came to Abraham, bringing Phicol, who commanded his troops.{h} “Whatever you do, God is on your side,” Abimelech said.

So here, in God’s name, give me your word that you will never cheat me, my children, or my grandchildren. I treated you with true friendship. Treat me and this land, where you are now a visitor, the same way.”
“I promise,” Abraham said.
Then Abraham complained to Abimelech about a well that Abimelech’s servants had grabbed.
“I have no idea who did that,” Abimelech replied. “You never told me, and today is the first I have heard of it.”
Abraham brought sheep and cattle as a gift to Abimelech, and the two of them made a formal treaty.{i}
Abraham then separated seven young ewes from the rest of the flock.
“Why did you set these seven lambs by themselves?” Abimelech asked.
“Accept these seven lambs from my hand,” Abraham said. “They will be your proof that I dug this well.”
So that place was named Beersheba,{j} because the two men made their solemn promise there.
Once the treaty was made at Beersheba, Abimelech and his commander Phicol returned to Philistine territory.{k}
At Beersheba, Abraham planted a tamarisk tree.{l} There he worshiped Yahweh, El Olam.{m}
Abraham stayed in Philistine country as a guest for a long time.

notes.text: The Hebrew verb means “visited” or “paid attention to.” It is often used when God acts to keep a promise.
Or “laugh at me.” The Septuagint says “will be glad with me.”
Hebrew metsacheq, which sounds like the name Isaac. It can mean playing, laughing, or mocking. The Septuagint adds “with her son Isaac.”
Literally “in Isaac your seed will be named.” Paul quotes this in Romans 9:7.
The Hebrew is unclear about whether the boy was put on her shoulder too. Ishmael was about 16 here. The Septuagint says he put the child on her shoulder.
The Septuagint says “the child cried out and wept,” which fits verse 17.
The Hebrew phrase is rare. It may mean “a young bowman.”
The Septuagint adds the name Ahuzzath, a friend of the king, here and in verse 32. The Hebrew gives that name only in 26:26.
Hebrew berit, “covenant.”
Beersheba means both “well of seven” and “well of the promise,” since the Hebrew words for “seven” and “swear” come from one root.
Records show the Philistines arriving on this coast about 1200 BC. The name may refer to earlier people of the same area, or it may be a later name used for readers’ sake.
A tamarisk is a tough desert tree. The Septuagint says “planted a field.”
El Olam means “the God who lasts forever.”

verses.text: Some time later God tested Abraham.{a} “Abraham!” God called. “I am here,” he answered.
God said, “Take Isaac, your son, your only one,{b} the one you love most. Travel to the land of Moriah.{c} On a hill I will point out to you, give him to me as a burnt offering.”{d}
Abraham was up at dawn. He saddled his donkey, took two servants and his son Isaac, and chopped wood for the offering. Then they started out for the place God had named.
On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the hill far ahead.
“Stay here with the donkey,” he told the young men. “The boy and I will walk up there and worship. Then we will come back to you.”{e}
Abraham loaded the wood for the offering onto Isaac’s shoulders. He himself carried the fire{f} and the knife. So the two of them went on together.
“Father,” Isaac said. “I am listening, son,” Abraham said. “We have the fire and the wood,” Isaac said, “but I do not see a lamb for the offering.”
“God will provide{g} the lamb himself, my son,” Abraham replied. They kept walking, side by side.
They came to the spot God had told him about. Abraham made an altar there and stacked the wood on it. Then he tied{h} up his son Isaac and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood.
Then Abraham reached for the knife and lifted it to kill his son.
At that moment the angel of Yahweh shouted from heaven, “Abraham! Abraham!” “I am here,” he answered.
“Do not touch the boy,” the angel said. “Do not hurt him at all. Now I know that you honor God, because you were willing to give me even your only son.”
Abraham glanced up. Behind him{i} a ram was tangled by its horns in a thicket.{j} He caught the ram and burned it as an offering in place of his son.
Abraham called that place Yahweh Yireh.{k} That is why people still say, “On Yahweh’s mountain it is provided.”{l}
The angel of Yahweh called out from heaven to Abraham once more.
“I have sworn by my own name,” Yahweh declares. “You did this, and you refused to keep your son back from me, your only son.
So I promise to bless you again and again. Your family will grow past counting, like the stars above and the sand on the seashore. They will conquer the gates{m} of their enemies.
Every nation on earth will receive a blessing{n} through your descendants, because you listened to my voice.”
Abraham went back to his servants. Together they traveled to Beersheba, and Abraham lived there.
Some time later a message came to Abraham: “Your brother Nahor and his wife Milcah have had sons.
They are Uz, the oldest; his brother Buz; Kemuel, the father of Aram;
Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel.”
Bethuel became the father of Rebekah.{o} Milcah bore these eight sons to Abraham’s brother Nahor.
Reumah, his concubine, was the mother of Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.

notes.text: Hebrew nissah, “tested” or “proved.” The writer tells us at the start that this is a test. Jewish tradition calls the chapter the Akedah, “the Binding.”
The Hebrew word yachid means “only” or “one of a kind.” Ishmael had been sent away. The Septuagint says “the beloved one.”

Second Chronicles 3:1 says Solomon built the temple on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem. The Septuagint says “the high land.” The name sounds like the Hebrew word for “see,” which is used again and again in this chapter.
Hebrew olah, “something that goes up.” It was an offering burned whole on the altar.
The Hebrew verb is plural: “we will come back.” Hebrews 11:19 says Abraham trusted that God could raise the dead.
Probably a pot of hot coals for starting the altar fire.
Literally “God will see to the lamb for himself.” In Hebrew, “see to” means “provide.” It prepares for the name in verse 14.
Hebrew aqad, found only here in the Bible.
Hebrew achar, “behind.” Some Hebrew copies and ancient translations read echad, “one ram.”
The Septuagint treats the Hebrew word for “thicket” as a name: “a plant of Sabek.”
Yahweh Yireh means “Yahweh will see to it” or “Yahweh will provide.” The Septuagint says “The Lord has seen.”
Or “On the mountain Yahweh will appear.” The Hebrew can be read more than one way.
The city gate stood for the whole city and its strength. The Septuagint says “the cities of their enemies.”
Or “will bless themselves.” Compare 12:3. Acts 3:25 quotes this as a promise to all peoples.
Rebekah means “a tied-up animal” or “a noose,” perhaps a pet name for a captivating girl. The meaning is uncertain. This note on her family prepares us for chapter 24.

verses.text: Sarah lived to be 127 years old.{a}
She died in Kiriath-arba,{b} which is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. Abraham came to mourn for her and cry over her body.
After a while he stood up from beside her and spoke to the Hittites:{c}
“I am an outsider living among you, a guest with no land of my own.{d} Sell me a piece of ground to use as a graveyard, so I can bury my wife and take her out of my sight.”
The Hittites replied,
“Please listen, sir. You are a powerful leader{e} among us. Choose our finest grave and bury her there. Not one of us will refuse you his grave.”
Abraham stood and bowed low to the Hittites, the people of that land.
“If you really are willing to let me bury my wife here,” he said, “then please speak for me to Ephron son of Zohar.
Machpelah{f} is a cave at the far end of Ephron’s field. Ask him to sell it to me for whatever it is truly worth, with all of you as witnesses. I need it as a family tomb.”
Ephron was seated among the Hittites. In front of everyone who passed through the city gate, he answered Abraham:
“Never, sir! Hear me. The field is yours, and the cave in it as well. Before my own people I make you this gift. Bury your wife.”{g}
Abraham bowed low again before the people of the land.
Abraham spoke to Ephron while the others listened: “I beg you, hear me. I insist on paying for the field. Accept my silver, and I will bury my wife there.”
Ephron replied,
“Sir, listen. That land is worth about 10 pounds of silver.{h} What is that between two men like us? Go and bury your wife.”
Abraham accepted the price. He weighed out for Ephron the amount he had named while the Hittites listened. It came to about 10 pounds of silver, by the weight that traders used.{i}
So Ephron’s field at Machpelah, across from Mamre (the field, the cave in it, and every tree inside its borders)
became Abraham’s own property. The Hittites at the city gate were the witnesses.
Then Abraham buried his wife Sarah in the cave in the field of Machpelah, across from Mamre (that is, Hebron), in Canaan.
So the field and its cave passed from the Hittites to Abraham as a place to bury the dead.{j}

notes.text: Literally “a hundred years and twenty years and seven years.” Sarah is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is given.
Kiriath-arba means “city of four.” It may refer to four clans or four villages. The Septuagint adds “which is in the valley.”
“Sons of Heth” (see 10:15) were a local Canaanite people, also called Hittites. They were probably not the same as the great Hittite empire far to the north.
Hebrew ger wetoshav, “a stranger and a settler,” someone who lives in a country but owns none of it. This cave becomes the first piece of the promised land that Abraham owns.
Literally “a prince of God,” a Hebrew way of saying “a very great prince.” The Septuagint says “a king from God.”
Machpelah may mean “double.” The Septuagint says “the double cave.”
Giving a gift was a polite part of bargaining. Abraham insists on paying so that nobody can dispute his ownership later.

Hebrew “400 shekels of silver.” A shekel was a weight, not a coin. At about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams) each, 400 shekels is about 10 pounds (4.6 kg). Weight standards differed from place to place. The price was very high. The Septuagint says “didrachms.”
Hebrew “400 shekels of silver” (about 10 pounds, 4.6 kg), literally “passing to the merchant,” meaning silver of standard weight.
This cave became the family tomb of Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob (25:9; 49:29-32; 50:13).

verses.text: Abraham had reached a great old age, and Yahweh had blessed everything in his life.
One day he spoke to the senior servant of his household, the man in charge of all his property. “Place your hand under my thigh,{a}” he said.
Promise me, with Yahweh as your witness, the God who rules the sky and the earth, that you will not pick a wife for my son from the local Canaanite girls.
You must travel to my old country, to my own family, and find Isaac a bride there.”
“Suppose she will not leave her home to come here,” the servant asked. “Must I then bring Isaac back to the country you left?”
“Never,” Abraham said. “Do not take my son there under any condition.

Yahweh, God of the sky, took me out of my father’s house and the land where I was born. He spoke to me and swore, ‘I will give this land to your family.’ He will send an angel in front of you, and from there you will bring back a wife for my son.
If she refuses to come, you are released{b} from your oath. But my son must not go back there.”
So the servant placed his hand under his master Abraham’s thigh and took the oath about this matter.
Then he loaded ten camels from his master’s herd with all sorts of fine presents and set out for Aram-naharaim,{c} to the town where Nahor’s family lived.
Near the town he let the camels kneel down by a well. The sun was setting, the hour when women walk out to fetch water.
“Yahweh, God of my master Abraham,” he prayed, “let things go well for me today. Be faithful{d} to my master Abraham.
See, I wait beside this spring while the girls of the town come to draw water.

I will ask one of them, ‘Would you lower your jar and let me drink?’ Suppose she replies, ‘Have a drink, and I will give water to your camels too.’ Then she is the one you picked for your servant Isaac. By this I will know you have been faithful to my master.”
He had not yet finished speaking when Rebekah appeared, carrying a water jar on her shoulder. She was the daughter of Bethuel, whose mother was Milcah, wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother.
The girl was beautiful to look at, and she was a virgin, untouched by any man.{e} She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and climbed back up.
The servant ran to meet her. “May I drink a little water from your jar?” he asked.
“Drink, sir,” she said, and she quickly tilted the jar down into her hands for him.
Once he had drunk his fill, she added, “I will keep drawing for your camels until all of them are satisfied.”
She hurried to pour the jar into the trough, then ran back for more, until she had watered every one of his camels.{f}
The man stood watching her without a word, wondering if Yahweh had made his journey a success.
When the camels had finished drinking, the man took out a gold nose ring that weighed about a fifth of an ounce. He also took two gold bracelets weighing about 4 ounces and put them on her wrists.{g}
“Whose daughter are you, please tell me?” he said. “Does your father have a place where we could stay the night?”
“My father is Bethuel,” she told him. “His parents were Milcah and Nahor.”
“We have lots of straw and feed,” she went on, “and room for you to sleep.”
The man knelt and bowed down to Yahweh.
“Blessed be Yahweh, the God of my master Abraham,” he said. “He has not stopped showing my master loyal love and truth.{h} Yahweh himself led me straight to my master’s family.”
The girl raced off to tell her mother’s household about these events.
Rebekah had a brother named Laban. He hurried out to the man at the spring.

He had seen the nose ring and the bracelets on his sister’s arms, and he had listened to Rebekah tell what the man had said. So he went to the man, who was still standing with his camels by the spring.
“Come in, you whom Yahweh has blessed!” Laban said. “Why wait outside? I have cleared a room for you and a place for the camels.”
So the man went into the house. Laban{i} unloaded the camels and gave them straw and feed, and he brought water so that the man and his companions could wash their feet.
Food was put in front of the servant, but he refused it. “Not until I have told you my errand,” he said. “Then say it,” Laban answered.
“I am Abraham’s servant,” the man began.
Yahweh has given my master great wealth. He has blessed him with flocks, herds, silver and gold, servants, maids, camels, and donkeys.
In her old age my master’s wife Sarah bore him a son.{j} My master has handed everything he owns to that boy.
He made me swear an oath: ‘You may not find a wife for my son among the Canaanite girls of the land where I live.
Go to my father’s house and my family, and find my son a wife there.’
“‘What if she will not follow me?’ I asked.
‘Yahweh, in whose presence I have lived,’ he answered, ‘will send his angel with you and make your journey succeed. You will find a wife for my son from my own relatives, from my father’s household.
Only when you reach my relatives, and they refuse you, will you be free from this oath. Then the curse{k} will not apply to you.’
“This day I arrived at the spring and prayed, ‘Yahweh, God of my master Abraham, if you really are making my journey a success,
here is what I ask. I am waiting at this spring. When a girl{l} comes out to draw water and I say, “May I have a little water from your jar?”
and she says to me, “Drink, and I will fetch water for your camels as well,” then she is the woman you have chosen for my master’s son.’
“I had barely finished that silent prayer when Rebekah came out, her jar on her shoulder. She walked down to the spring and filled it. I said to her, ‘Please let me drink.’
At once she lowered her jar from her shoulder. ‘Drink,’ she said, ‘and I will give your camels water too.’ I drank, and she watered the camels.
Then I asked, ‘Who is your father?’ ‘Bethuel,’ she said, ‘the son of Nahor and Milcah.’ So I fastened the ring to her nose and the bracelets to her wrists.
I knelt and worshiped Yahweh. I praised Yahweh, the God of my master Abraham, who had guided me on the right road to find my master’s niece{m} for his son.
Now tell me: will you show loyal love and truth to my master or not? Whatever your answer, tell me, so I know which way to turn.”
Laban and Bethuel{n} answered, “This comes from Yahweh. It is not for us to say good or bad.{o}
Rebekah is here. Take her with you, and let her become the wife of your master’s son, as Yahweh has said.”
The servant of Abraham listened, and then he lay face down on the ground to honor Yahweh.
Next he took out jewelry of silver and of gold, along with clothing, and gave it all to Rebekah. To her brother and her mother he gave valuable gifts as well.
He and the men with him ate and drank, and they spent the night there. When they got up the next morning, he said, “Let me return to my master.”
But her brother and mother replied, “Let Rebekah remain with us for ten days or so.{p} After that she can go.”
“Do not make me wait,” he said. “Yahweh has given me a successful trip. Send me on my way to my master.”
“Let us call the girl and see what she wants,” they said.{q}
They called Rebekah and asked, “Will you go with this man?” “Yes,” she said, “I will go.”
So they let their sister Rebekah leave with her nurse{r} and with Abraham’s servant and his men.
This was the blessing they spoke over Rebekah: “Sister, may you become the mother of thousands upon thousands. May your descendants capture the gates of their enemies.”
Rebekah and her young women got up, climbed onto the camels, and rode after the man. And so the servant took Rebekah and went on his way.
Isaac, meanwhile, had come from the direction of Beer-lahai-roi,{s} since he lived in the Negev.
Toward evening he went out into the field to stroll and think.{t} He glanced up and saw camels approaching.
Rebekah looked up and saw Isaac. She climbed down from her camel
and asked the servant, “Who is that man in the field, walking to meet us?” “That is my master,” the servant said. So she took her veil and covered her face.
The servant told Isaac the whole story of his trip.
Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah.{u} He married Rebekah, and he loved her. In her he found comfort after his mother’s death.

notes.text: This was a way of making a solemn promise (also in 47:29). “Thigh” may be a polite word for the body part linked to children and to the circumcision sign.
Literally “clean” or “innocent.” He would carry no guilt if he could not keep the promise.
Aram-naharaim means “Aram of the two rivers,” the land around the upper Euphrates. The Septuagint says “Mesopotamia.”
Hebrew chesed, loyal and steady love that keeps a promise. It is a key word in this chapter (verses 14, 27, 49).
Hebrew betulah, a girl old enough to marry. The next sentence makes clear she was a virgin.
A camel can drink a huge amount after a long trip. Watering ten of them was hard work and showed how generous and strong Rebekah was.

Hebrew “a beka (half a shekel) in weight,” about a fifth of an ounce (5.7 g), and “ten shekels of gold in weight,” about 4 ounces (115 g), counting a shekel as about 0.4 ounce (11.5 g). Verse 47 shows the ring was for her nose. The Septuagint says “gold earrings that weighed a drachma.”
Hebrew chesed we’emet, “loyal love and truth.” God is often described this way (Exodus 34:6).
The Hebrew just says “he unloaded.” Laban is the likely one, though some readers think it was the servant.
Literally “after her old age.” The Samaritan Pentateuch is reported to say “his old age.”
Hebrew alah, the curse that falls on someone who breaks an oath. The Septuagint says “my curse.”
Hebrew almah, “young woman.” The same word is used in Isaiah 7:14. Here it describes Rebekah, whom verse 16 calls a virgin.
Literally “brother’s daughter.” Rebekah was really the granddaughter of Abraham’s brother Nahor.

Mentioning Bethuel here is surprising, since Laban and his mother act for the family in verses 28, 53, and 55. Some scholars think Bethuel’s name was added later, or that Josephus was right that he was dead.
Literally “we cannot speak bad or good to you,” an idiom for “we can say nothing against it.”
Literally “days or ten,” an odd phrase. It may mean “about ten days” or even “a year or ten months.” The Septuagint says “about ten days.”
Literally “ask her mouth.” The family wanted her agreement.
She is named Deborah in 35:8. The Septuagint says “her belongings.”
Beer-lahai-roi means “well of the living God who watches over me.” It is the well where God met Hagar (16:14).
Hebrew lasuach, a rare word. It may mean “to walk,” “to think deeply,” or “to pray.” The Septuagint says “to meditate.”
The Hebrew reads “into the tent Sarah his mother,” which looks shortened. The meaning is clear: Rebekah took the place of honor that had been Sarah’s.

verses.text: Abraham took another wife, named Keturah.{a}
She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
Sheba and Dedan were sons of Jokshan. From Dedan came the Asshurim, the Letushim, and the Leummim.
Midian{b} was the father of Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All of these came from Keturah.
Abraham left everything he owned to Isaac.
To the sons born to his concubines,{c} Abraham gave gifts while he was still alive. He sent them away from his son Isaac to live in the east.
Abraham lived 175 years in all.
He took his last breath and died in a good old age, content with a full life.{d} He was gathered to his ancestors.{e}
His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, across from Mamre.
Abraham had bought that field from the Hittites. He was buried there with his wife Sarah.
After Abraham died, God blessed Isaac, his son, who was living at Beer-lahai-roi.
This is the family history{f} of Ishmael, the son Abraham had with Hagar, Sarah’s Egyptian servant.
Here are Ishmael’s sons by name, in order of birth: first Nebaioth, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
Mishma, Dumah, Massa,
Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
Those were Ishmael’s sons, and they gave their names to villages and camps.{g} Twelve of them became tribal chiefs.{h}
Ishmael died at the age of 137, gathered to his people.
His descendants settled in the land from Havilah to Shur, which is east of Egypt on the road toward Assyria. They lived in tension{i} with all their relatives.
This is the family history of Isaac, the son of Abraham. Abraham was Isaac’s father.
Isaac was 40 when he married Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean from Paddan-aram{j} and the sister of Laban the Aramean.
Isaac prayed to Yahweh for his wife, who could not have children. Yahweh answered him, and Rebekah became pregnant.
The babies pushed against each other{k} inside her. “If this is how it is, why go on living?”{l} she said. She went to ask Yahweh about it.
Yahweh answered, “There are two nations inside you. Two different peoples will come apart from your body. One will be the stronger people, and the older son will serve the younger.”{m}
When her time came, the babies were indeed twins.
The first came out red,{n} covered with hair all over like a coat. They named him Esau.{o}
Then his brother came out, holding on to Esau’s heel. So he was named Jacob.{p} Isaac was 60 when the twins were born.
As the boys grew, Esau turned into an expert hunter who loved the open country. Jacob was a calm man{q} who preferred life in the tents.
Isaac loved Esau, since the wild game was to his taste,{r} but Rebekah loved Jacob.
Once, Jacob was boiling a stew when Esau arrived from the open country, exhausted.
“Quick, let me gulp down some of that red stew,” Esau said. “I am starving!” That is why people call him Edom.{s}
“First sell me your rights as the oldest son,”{t} Jacob said.
“I am about to die,” Esau said. “What good are those rights to me?”
“Promise me first,” Jacob said. Esau made the promise and sold his rights as oldest son to Jacob.
Jacob served Esau bread and lentil stew. Esau ate and drank, stood up, and walked off. He showed how little he valued the rights of the oldest son.{u}

notes.text: Or “had taken.” The Hebrew does not say when this marriage happened. First Chronicles 1:32 calls Keturah a concubine. Her name may mean “incense.”
Midian became the father of the Midianites, among whom Moses later lived (Exodus 2:15-22).
Probably Hagar and Keturah.
Hebrew zaqen wesave’a, “old and satisfied.” The Septuagint says “full of days.”
This phrase means joining one’s ancestors in death. It is different from burial (verse 9).
Hebrew toledot, “family history.” This word marks the main sections of Genesis.
Hebrew tirah, a camp of tents set in a ring.
The twelve chiefs match the promise in 17:20. Names such as Kedar, Tema, Dumah, and Nebaioth are known from records as tribes or oases of northern Arabia.
Or “to the east of,” as in 16:12. The Hebrew literally says “he fell on the face of.” The Septuagint says “he lived in front of all his brothers.”
Paddan-aram probably means “plain of Aram,” the area around Haran. The Septuagint says “Syrian Mesopotamia.”
Hebrew ratsats, “crushed one another,” a rough word. The Septuagint says “jumped.”
Literally “If so, why this I?” The Hebrew is short. It may mean “Why is this happening to me?” or “Why do I live?”

The Hebrew is very short and can be read two ways: “the older will serve the younger” or “the older, the younger will serve.” Paul quotes the first reading in Romans 9:12. The message is about two nations, Israel and Edom, as well as two brothers.
Hebrew admoni, “reddish,” a play on the name Edom.
The text does not explain Esau’s name. “Hairy” (se’ar) sounds like Seir, the hill country where Edom later lived (32:3). Esau may mean “hairy” or “made.”
Jacob (Ya’aqov) sounds like the Hebrew for “heel.” The name may mean “may God protect,” but here it is tied to grabbing a heel, and later to tripping someone up (27:36).
Hebrew tam, often “blameless” or “whole.” Here it may mean “gentle” or “settled,” the opposite of a hunter. The Septuagint says “a simple man.”
Literally “because game was in his mouth.”
Edom means “red.” The Hebrew says “the red, this red,” showing how hungry and hurried Esau was.
The firstborn son received a double share of the inheritance and became the family leader (Deuteronomy 21:17).
Hebrews 12:16 uses this story as a warning against treating holy things lightly.

verses.text: Hunger came to the land, just as in the days of Abraham. So Isaac traveled to Gerar, where Abimelech ruled the Philistines.{a}
Yahweh showed himself to Isaac there. “Do not go down into Egypt,” he said. “Settle in the country I will tell you about.
Stay in this land as a foreigner. I will be with you and bless you. To you and your family I will give all of these territories, keeping the oath I made to your father Abraham.
I will make your family as countless as the stars of the sky, and I will hand them all these territories. Through your descendants every nation of the earth will find blessing,{b}
because Abraham listened to me and did what I asked. He kept my orders, my rules, and my teachings.”{c}
So Isaac settled in Gerar.
The local men asked him about Rebekah. “She is my sister,” he told them. He was afraid to say “wife,” thinking, “These men could kill me for her.” She was a strikingly beautiful woman.
Some time later, Abimelech the king happened to look down from his window. He saw Isaac fondling{d} Rebekah.
Abimelech summoned Isaac. “She is your wife, is she not?” he demanded. “Why did you tell us she was your sister?” “I feared that I might be killed because of her,” Isaac answered.
“What is this you have done to us?” Abimelech said. “One of my people could easily have slept with your wife, and you would have made us guilty.”
Abimelech then warned all his people: “Whoever lays a hand on this man or his wife must die.”
Isaac planted crops in that land. That year he gathered a hundred times what he had sowed,{e} because Yahweh blessed him.
His wealth kept growing until he was very rich.
His flocks, his herds, and his household of workers kept growing, and the Philistines began to envy him.
They took all the wells that the servants of Abraham had dug in his lifetime, and they plugged them with dirt.
Abimelech told Isaac, “Leave our area. You have grown far stronger than we are.”
Isaac moved away from there and set up camp in the Gerar valley,{f} where he made his home.
Isaac dug out again the wells from the days of his father Abraham, which the Philistines had filled in after Abraham’s death. He called each well by the name Abraham had given it.
Isaac’s servants dug in the valley and found a spring of fresh water.{g}
The herdsmen of Gerar argued with Isaac’s herdsmen, claiming, “This water belongs to us.” So Isaac named that well Esek,{h} meaning “argument,” since they had picked a fight with him.
His men dug another well, and they fought over that one too. He named it Sitnah.{i}
He left and dug yet another well. No one quarreled over this one, so he called it Rehoboth.{j} “At last Yahweh has given us space,” he said. “We will thrive in this country.”
From that place he went on up to Beersheba.
That night Yahweh appeared to him. “I am the God of Abraham, your father,” he said. “Fear nothing, for I am with you. For the sake of my servant Abraham I will bless you and increase your family.”
Isaac built an altar there and worshiped Yahweh. He pitched his tent, and his servants dug a well.
Abimelech arrived from Gerar, accompanied by Ahuzzath{k} his counselor and by Phicol, who led his army.
“Why have you come to me?” Isaac asked. “You hated me and sent me away.”
They answered, “We could see clearly that Yahweh is with you. We decided we should have a sworn agreement between us. Let us make a treaty with you.
Swear that you will do us no harm. We have never hurt you. We treated you well and let you leave in peace. Clearly Yahweh is blessing you.”
Isaac prepared a feast for them, and they dined together.
At dawn the next day the men swore oaths to each other. Isaac saw them off, and they went away in peace.
On that same day Isaac’s servants came to him with news about the well they had been digging. “We found water!” they announced.{l}
Isaac called it Shibah.{m} This is why the town is named Beersheba to this day.
At the age of 40, Esau took two Hittite wives: Judith, whose father was Beeri, and Basemath, whose father was Elon.{n}
These women made life bitter{o} for Isaac and Rebekah.

notes.text: For the Philistines, see the note on 21:32. This Abimelech may have followed the king in chapter 20, since the name may be a royal title.
Or “will bless themselves,” as in 22:18.
This verse uses four words for God’s instructions. The last one is torah, “teaching.” It shows that Abraham was faithful long before the Law of Moses.
Hebrew metsacheq, from the same root as the name Isaac (“he laughs”). Here it means a husband and wife playing together lovingly.
Literally “found a hundred measures.” The Septuagint says “a hundredfold of barley.”
Hebrew nachal, a stream valley that may be dry except in the rainy season.
Literally “living water,” meaning water that flows from a spring.
Esek means “fight” or “quarrel.” The Septuagint translates it “Injury.”
Sitnah means “hostility” or “accusation.” It has the same root as satan, “enemy.” The Septuagint says “Enmity.”
Rehoboth means “wide places” or “room.”
Literally “his friend,” probably a title for a royal adviser.
The Septuagint says “We have not found water,” reading the Hebrew word lo as “not” instead of “to him.”
Shibah means “oath” or “seven” (compare 21:31).
The lists of Esau’s wives in 28:9 and 36:2-3 give some different names.
Literally “a bitterness of spirit.”

subheads.6: Isaac says Rebekah is his sister

verses.text: Isaac was now an old man, and his sight had faded until he was blind. He summoned Esau, his older son. “Son!” he called. “Here I am,” Esau said.
“I am old now,” Isaac said. “I could die any day.
Take your hunting gear,{a} your bow and arrows, and go out to the open country. Bring me back some wild meat.
Make it into the tasty dish I love, and bring it to me. When I have eaten, I will bless you myself,{b} before I die.”
Rebekah had overheard Isaac’s words to Esau. As soon as Esau went off into the countryside to hunt game,
she turned to her son Jacob. “I overheard your father telling your brother Esau,
‘Bring me game and prepare a meal for me. After I eat, I will bless you before Yahweh and then die.’
Now, my son, listen and do just what I say.
Go to the flock and fetch two fine young goats. I will turn them into the meal your father loves.
You take it in to him. When he has eaten, he will bless you before he dies.”
“Esau, my brother, has hairy skin,” Jacob objected, “and mine is smooth.
If my father touches me, he will see that I am tricking him,{c} and I will earn myself a curse rather than a blessing.”
“May the curse come down on me, my son,” his mother answered. “Just do what I tell you and bring me those goats.”
He fetched them and gave them to his mother, who cooked the delicious meal his father loved.
Rebekah then took out the finest clothes belonging to Esau, her older son, which were stored in the house, and dressed Jacob in them.
With the goat skins she covered his hands and the smooth part of his neck.
She put the food and the fresh bread she had made into Jacob’s hands.
Jacob went to his father. “Father?” he said. “Yes, I am here,” Isaac said. “Which of my sons are you?”
Jacob said, “I am Esau, your oldest son. I did what you asked. Please sit up and eat the meat I caught, and then give me your blessing.”
“How did you find it so quickly, my son?” Isaac asked. “Yahweh your God helped me,” Jacob said.
Then Isaac said, “Come closer, my son. Let me feel you and find out if you are really my son Esau.”
Jacob stepped up to his father. Isaac ran his hands over him and said, “That is Jacob’s voice, yet the hands are the hands of Esau.”
He did not recognize Jacob, because his hands were as hairy as Esau’s. So he went ahead and blessed him.{d}
“Are you truly my son Esau?” “I am,” Jacob said.
Isaac said, “Bring me the meat, my son, so I can eat it and give you my blessing.” Jacob brought it, and Isaac ate. Jacob brought wine too, and Isaac drank.
Then Isaac, his father, said to him, “Come here, my son, and kiss me.”
Jacob stepped up and kissed him. Isaac smelled his clothes, and blessed him with these words: “Ah, my son’s smell is the smell of a field that Yahweh has blessed.{e}
May God give you heaven’s dew and earth’s richness, with grain and new wine in plenty.{f}
Let nations serve you and peoples bow low to you. Be lord over your brothers, and let your mother’s sons bow down to you. Cursed be those who curse you, and blessed be those who bless you.”
Isaac had barely finished blessing him, and Jacob had just left, when his brother Esau came back from hunting.
Esau also cooked a tasty meal and brought it to his father. “Father, sit up and eat some of your son’s meat,” he said. “Then give me your blessing.”
“Who are you?” his father Isaac asked. “I am Esau, your oldest son,” he answered.
Isaac trembled violently.{g} “Who, then, hunted game and brought it to me?” he asked. “I finished eating before you arrived, and I blessed him. And the blessing stays with him.”
When Esau heard his father’s words, he cried out loudly and bitterly. “Bless me too, Father!” he begged.
“Your brother came and tricked me,” Isaac said. “He took your blessing.”

“Is that why he is called Jacob?”{h} Esau cried. “Twice now he has tricked me! He seized my place as oldest son, and now he has seized my blessing!”{i} Then he pleaded, “Have you not kept a blessing back for me?”
Isaac replied, “I have made him lord over you, and I have given all his relatives to him as servants. I have supplied him with grain and new wine. What is left for me to give you, my son?”
“Father, do you have only one blessing?” Esau said. “Bless me too, Father!” Esau began to sob.{j}
His father Isaac replied, “You will live away from the rich land, away from the dew that falls from heaven.{k}
You will live by your sword and be your brother’s servant. But when you break free, you will throw his yoke off your neck.”{l}
Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. He thought, “My father’s time of mourning is near. Then I will kill my brother Jacob.”
When Rebekah was told what her older son Esau was saying, she called Jacob and told him, “Your brother Esau is consoling himself with the thought of killing you.
So now, my son, listen to what I say. Run away to my brother Laban in Haran.
Live with him for a while, until your brother’s temper has cooled.
When he is no longer angry and has forgotten what you did, I will send for you. Why should I lose both of you in one day?”{m}
Then Rebekah said to Isaac, “These Hittite women{n} have made me sick of living. If Jacob marries a local girl like them, my life will not be worth living.”

notes.text: Hebrew keli, “equipment” or “weapons.” The word for “quiver” is found only here in the Bible, and its meaning comes from old tradition.
Literally “my soul may bless you,” meaning “I myself,” a full and deliberate blessing. People then believed that a dying father’s blessing could not be undone.
Or “a cheat.” The Septuagint says “someone with bad intentions.”
This line may sum up the story before the actual blessing in verses 27-29.
The Septuagint says “the smell of a full field.”
Hebrew tirosh, freshly pressed wine.
Literally “trembled with a great trembling.”
Jacob (Ya’aqov) sounds like the verb for “grab the heel,” “cheat,” or “trip up.” Compare 25:26.
A wordplay in Hebrew: bekhorah, “birthright,” and berakhah, “blessing.”
The Septuagint adds “And Isaac was troubled” before Esau weeps. These words are not in the Hebrew.
Or “Your home will be in the rich soil and under the dew of the sky.” The Hebrew word min can mean “far from” or “a share of.” The sense is probably the first, since Edom’s land was dry.
The Hebrew verb is unclear. It may mean “roam free,” “get restless,” or “break loose.” See 2 Kings 8:20-22, where Edom rebels against Judah.
That is, Jacob would be killed by Esau, and Esau would be condemned for murder (9:6) or forced to run away.
“Daughters of Heth” were local Canaanite women (10:15; 23:3). Esau’s Hittite wives are named in 26:34-35.

verses.text: Isaac called Jacob in, blessed him, and gave him these orders: “You are not to marry a Canaanite girl.
Set out at once for Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel, your mother’s father. Find yourself a wife there, one of the daughters of your uncle Laban, your mother’s brother.
May El Shaddai{a} bless you. May he give you children, and make you so numerous that you become a company of peoples.{b}
May he pass on to you and your descendants the blessing he gave to Abraham, so that you will take possession of the land where you now live as a stranger, the land God gave to Abraham.”
Isaac sent Jacob away, and he traveled to Paddan-aram, to Laban the Aramean, the son of Bethuel and brother of Rebekah. Rebekah was the mother of Jacob and Esau.
Esau learned that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to find a wife. When he blessed him, Isaac had told him not to marry a Canaanite girl.
Esau also learned that Jacob had obeyed his parents and set out for Paddan-aram.
It was clear to Esau that the Canaanite women did not please his father Isaac.
So Esau went to Ishmael, Abraham’s son, and took Mahalath{c} as another wife. She was Ishmael’s daughter and the sister of Nebaioth. He already had other wives.
Meanwhile, Jacob left Beersheba and headed toward Haran.
Evening found him at a certain spot,{d} and he decided to sleep there since the sun was gone. He picked up one of the stones lying around, put it under his head, and lay down.
Then he dreamed. A stairway{e} was standing on the earth, and the top of it reached into heaven. God’s angels were going up and down along it.{f}
And there was Yahweh, standing{g} above it. “I am Yahweh,” he said. “I am the God of Abraham, your father, and of Isaac. I am giving you and your descendants the ground you are lying on.

Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth in number. You will break out to the west and the east, to the north and the south. Every family on earth will be blessed through you and your offspring.{h}
Know this: I am with you. I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. I will never abandon you until all I have promised you is done.”
Jacob woke up. “Yahweh is really in this place,” he said, “and I did not know it!”
Terrified, he whispered, “This place is awesome! It is nothing less than God’s house, the gate to heaven.”
Early the next morning Jacob took the stone he had put under his head, stood it on end as a pillar,{i} and poured oil over its top.
He named that place Bethel.{j} (The city had been called Luz before that.){k}
Then Jacob made a vow: “If God stays with me and guards me on this trip, and gives me food to eat and clothes to wear,
and if I get back safely to my father’s house, then Yahweh will be my God.{l}
This stone that I stood up as a pillar will be a house for God. And I promise to give you a tenth of everything you give me.”

notes.text: El Shaddai is often translated “God Almighty.” See the note on 17:1. The Septuagint says “my God.”
Hebrew qehal ammim, “an assembly of peoples.” The word qahal was later used for Israel gathered to worship. The Septuagint says “gatherings of nations.”
Mahalath is called Basemath in 36:3. The Septuagint spells it “Maeleth.”
Literally “the place,” perhaps pointing to a known holy site. This word comes back again and again in the story.
Hebrew sullam, found only here. It could be a ladder or a ramp of steps like those on ancient temple towers (compare 11:4). The Septuagint says “ladder.”
Or “on him,” meaning on Jacob. Jesus refers to this in John 1:51.
Or “standing beside him.” The Septuagint says “the Lord stood on it.”
Or “will bless themselves.” See the note on 12:3. The Septuagint says “all the tribes of the earth.”
Hebrew matsevah, a standing stone set up as a memorial or a marker of a holy place. Later law banned such pillars when they were used to worship other gods (Deuteronomy 16:22).
Bethel means “house of God.”
The Septuagint joins the Hebrew words for “but Luz” into one name, “Ulam-luz.”
Or “and if Yahweh will be my God, then this stone...” The Hebrew can be divided so that the “if” continues into this part.

subheads.16: A stone, an oil, and a vow

verses.text: Jacob set out again{a} and came to the country of the eastern peoples.
Out in the open he spotted a well. Three flocks of sheep were resting beside it, because the animals drank from this well. A large stone sealed the mouth of it.
The shepherds waited until all the flocks had arrived. Then they rolled the stone off the well, gave the sheep water, and put the stone back.
“Friends, where do you come from?” Jacob asked. “We are from Haran,” they said.
“Do you know Laban, the grandson{b} of Nahor?” he asked. “We do,” they said.
“Is he well?”{c} Jacob asked. “Quite well,” they said. “And that is his daughter Rachel now, coming up with the flock.”
“The day is still long,” Jacob said, “and it is not yet time to bring the animals together. Give the sheep a drink and let them go back to pasture.”
“We are not allowed,” they replied. “Not until every flock has come. Then the stone is moved off, and we water the sheep.”
He was still speaking with them when Rachel came up with her father’s sheep, for she tended them herself.
Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of his mother’s brother Laban, with Laban’s sheep. He went to the well, rolled the stone away, and watered his uncle Laban’s flock.
Then Jacob kissed Rachel and cried out loud for joy.
Jacob told Rachel that he was a kinsman of her father,{d} Rebekah’s son. She raced off to tell her father.
The moment Laban heard that his nephew Jacob had come, he ran to greet him. He threw his arms around him, kissed him, and took him home. Then Jacob told Laban everything that had happened.
“You are my own flesh and blood!” Laban told him, and Jacob stayed with him for a full month.{e}
Then Laban said, “Just because you are my relative, should you work for me for nothing? Tell me what wages you want.”
Laban had two daughters. The older was named Leah and the younger was named Rachel.
Leah had gentle eyes,{f} but Rachel had a lovely figure and a lovely face.{g}
Jacob was in love with Rachel. “I will serve you seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter,” he offered.
“I would rather give her to you than to a stranger,” Laban said. “Stay here with me.”
So Jacob worked seven years to win Rachel. Because he loved her so much, it seemed like only a few days.
Then Jacob told Laban, “The time is finished. Hand over my wife, so I can marry her.”
Laban invited all the people of the place to a wedding banquet.
When evening came, though, Laban took Leah, his daughter, to Jacob, and Jacob lay with her.{h}
Laban also assigned his maid Zilpah to Leah, his daughter, as her servant.
When morning came, there was Leah! “What have you done to me?” Jacob said to Laban. “I worked for you to win Rachel! Why did you fool me?”{i}
Laban said, “In our country the younger daughter is never married before the older one.
Finish this one’s wedding week,{j} and we will give you the younger one too, if you promise to work for me another seven years.”
Jacob did that. He completed Leah’s wedding week, and afterward Laban gave him Rachel his daughter as a wife.
To Rachel his daughter, Laban gave his maid Bilhah as her servant.
Jacob slept with Rachel as well, and he loved her more than Leah. He worked for Laban another seven years.
Yahweh saw that Leah was not loved,{k} so he let her have children. Rachel had none.
Leah conceived and bore a son, and she called him Reuben.{l} “Yahweh has noticed my misery,” she said. “Surely now my husband will love me.”
She conceived again and bore another son. “Yahweh listened when I was unloved,” she said, “and has given me this one also.” She called him Simeon.{m}
She became pregnant again and had a third son. “Now at last my husband will stay close to me,” she said, “since I have given him three sons.” So she named him Levi.{n}
She conceived yet again and bore a son. “Now I will thank Yahweh,” she said, and she called him Judah.{o} After that she stopped bearing children for a time.

notes.text: Literally “Jacob lifted up his feet.”
“Son” here means “grandson” or “descendant.” Laban was Nahor’s grandson (24:29).
Literally “Is there peace (shalom) for him?”
Literally “brother.” Jacob was really Laban’s nephew.
Literally “a month of days.”
Hebrew rakkot, “tender,” “soft,” or “weak.” It may be praise for gentle eyes, or a contrast with Rachel’s beauty. The Septuagint says “weak.” Leah and Rachel may mean “wild cow” and “ewe.”
Literally “beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance.”
The bride was probably veiled (compare 24:65), and it was dark.
Hebrew rimmitani, from the same root as the “trick” (mirmah) Jacob used to get Esau’s blessing (27:35). The cheater is cheated.
The wedding feast lasted seven days (compare Judges 14:12).
Literally “hated,” a Hebrew way of saying “loved less” (compare verse 30).
Reuben sounds like the Hebrew for “See, a son!” and like Leah’s words “he has seen my sorrow.”
Simeon sounds like the Hebrew for “he has heard.”
Levi sounds like the Hebrew for “he will be joined.”
Judah sounds like the Hebrew for “I will praise.”

verses.text: When Rachel realized she had borne Jacob no children, she became envious of her sister. “Give me sons, or I am as good as dead!”{a} she cried to Jacob.
Jacob flared up at her. “Do I take God’s place?” he said. “He is the one who has denied you children.”
“Take my maid Bilhah,” she said. “Lie with her, so she can bear a child for me to hold on my knees.{b} Through her I too may have a family.”{c}
She gave Jacob her maid Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob lay with her.
Bilhah conceived and bore him a son.
“God has been my judge and has ruled for me,” said Rachel. “He listened to my plea and gave me a son.” That is why she called him Dan.{d}
Bilhah, Rachel’s maid, conceived again and bore Jacob another son.
“I have wrestled hard with my sister{e} and have won,” said Rachel, and she called him Naphtali.
Leah saw that she had stopped bearing children, so she took her maid Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as another wife.
Leah’s servant Zilpah gave Jacob a son.
“What good luck!”{f} Leah said, and she named him Gad.
Leah’s servant Zilpah gave Jacob a second son.
“I am so happy! The women will say I am blessed,” Leah exclaimed, and she called him Asher.{g}

In the season of the wheat harvest, Reuben was out in the fields, where he came across some mandrakes.{h} He took them to Leah, his mother. “Please share some of your son’s mandrakes with me,” Rachel said to Leah.
“Was it too little to take my husband from me?” Leah replied. “Do you want my son’s mandrakes as well?” “Then let him sleep with you tonight,” said Rachel, “in return for your son’s mandrakes.”

That evening, as Jacob came home from the fields, Leah went out to greet him. “You will sleep with me tonight,” she said. “I have paid for you with my son’s mandrakes.” So he slept with her that night.
God heard Leah and answered. She became pregnant, and Jacob had a fifth son by her.
“God has rewarded me for handing my maid to my husband,” said Leah, and she called him Issachar.{i}
Leah became pregnant again, and Jacob had a sixth son by her.
“God has given me a fine present,” Leah said. “Now my husband will honor me,{j} for I have borne him six sons.” And she called him Zebulun.
After that she bore a daughter and called her Dinah.{k}
Then God thought of Rachel again. He listened to her prayer and opened her womb.
She became pregnant and had a son. “God has taken away my shame,” she said.
She called him Joseph,{l} saying, “May Yahweh add another son to me.”
Soon after Rachel bore Joseph, Jacob spoke to Laban. “Send me away, so that I may return to my own land.
Give me my wives and children, whom I have worked for, and let me leave. You know how hard I have worked for you.”
“If you can spare me a moment of your good will,” Laban said, “I have noticed from signs{m} that Yahweh has blessed me because of you.”
He added, “Name your pay, and I will give it.”
“You know how I served you,” Jacob answered, “and how your livestock fared in my care.
What little you had before I came has grown into a huge amount. Yahweh has blessed you in everything I have done.{n} Now, when do I get to do something for my own household?”
“What can I pay you?” Laban asked. “Nothing at all,” Jacob said. “Do just one thing for me, and I will take your flock back out and tend it.
Today I will pass through your entire flock. Take out of it every speckled or spotted sheep, every black lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat. Those will be my wages.{o}
In the future my honesty will speak for me. When you come to check my pay, any goat of mine that is not speckled or spotted, and any lamb that is not dark, will count as stolen.”
“Good,” said Laban. “Let it be as you have said.”

That same day, however, Laban removed the striped or spotted male goats and every speckled or spotted female goat, any with white on it, and all the dark lambs. He gave them to his sons to look after.
He put a three-day walk between himself and Jacob, while Jacob looked after the rest of Laban’s flocks.
Jacob took fresh sticks of poplar, almond, and plane{p} and peeled white stripes in them by stripping the bark.
He placed the peeled sticks where the flocks would see them, in the troughs and water channels where the animals came to drink. When they came to drink, they mated.
They mated in front of the branches, and their young were striped, speckled, or spotted.{q}
Jacob separated the lambs. He made the rest of the flock face the striped and dark animals in Laban’s flock. He kept his own animals in separate herds and did not mix them with Laban’s.
Whenever the strong animals were mating, Jacob put the branches in the troughs where they could see them, so they would mate in front of the branches.
With the weaker animals, he left the sticks out. So Laban ended up with the feeble animals and Jacob with the sturdy ones.{r}
So the man grew exceedingly rich. He owned large flocks, servants of both sexes, camels, and donkeys.

notes.text: Literally “if not, I am dying.” Rachel later dies giving birth to her second son (35:16-19).
This was a way of adopting a child or claiming it as one’s own (compare 48:12; 50:23).
Literally “I will be built up,” a wordplay on the Hebrew for “son.” See the note on 16:2.
Dan sounds like the Hebrew for “he has judged.” The Septuagint says “God has given judgment for me.”
Literally “with wrestlings of God I have wrestled,” a Hebrew way of saying “mighty wrestlings.” Naphtali sounds like the Hebrew for “I have wrestled.”
The written Hebrew reads begad, “with good luck.” The Masoretic reading tradition divides it as ba gad, “luck has come.” Gad was also the name of a god of luck (Isaiah 65:11).
Asher sounds like the Hebrew for “happy” or “blessed.”
Hebrew duda’im, a plant whose root and fruit were thought to help women have children. The name sounds like the Hebrew for “love.”
Issachar sounds like the Hebrew for “wages” or “hire” (see verse 16).
Or “will live with me.” Zebulun sounds like the Hebrew for “gift” and for a rare verb meaning “honor” or “live with.”
Dinah’s name comes from the same root as Dan. It is not explained. Her story is told in chapter 34.
Joseph sounds like the Hebrew for “he has taken away” (verse 23) and for “may he add.”
The Hebrew word usually means “I have practiced fortune-telling” (compare 44:5). Some translate it “I have become rich.” The Septuagint says “I would take it as a good sign.”
Literally “at my foot.”
In that region most sheep were white and most goats dark, so speckled, spotted, and dark animals would be few. The Septuagint has Jacob take “every gray sheep among the rams.”
The trees are not certain. Hebrew livneh, “poplar,” sounds like lavan, “white,” and like the name Laban. The wordplay runs through the passage.
Herders then believed that what a mother saw while mating could mark her young. Jacob later gives God the credit, not his method (31:9-12).
The meaning of “strong” and “weak” is unclear. It may mean healthy and sickly animals, or animals mating in different seasons.
